label: Manhattan distance and rectilinear geometry
lesson:
# Manhattan distance and rectilinear geometry

Layout geometry is rectilinear: almost every wire, cell outline and via is a polygon whose edges run horizontally or vertically, on an integer grid. In that world the natural distance between two points is not the straight line but the Manhattan, or $L_1$, distance: the length of the shortest path that moves only along the axes. Wirelength estimates, routing costs, Steiner trees and placement objectives are all built on it, so a tool designer reaches for it before any other metric.

## The L1 metric

For points $p = (x_1, y_1)$ and $q = (x_2, y_2)$ the Manhattan distance is

$$d_1(p, q) = |x_1 - x_2| + |y_1 - y_2|.$$

It is a true metric: zero only for equal points, symmetric, and it obeys the triangle inequality. It is also the exact length of any monotone staircase wire from $p$ to $q$, which is why a router's lower bound for a two-pin net is $d_1$. Example: pins at $(120, 40)$ and $(35, 210)$ nm are $85 + 170 = 255$ nm apart. Its relatives matter too. The Chebyshev distance $d_\infty = \max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)$ appears in square-metric spacing checks, and rotating coordinates by 45 degrees, $u = x + y$, $v = x - y$, turns $d_1$ into $d_\infty$, a trick used by nearest-neighbour and Voronoi algorithms for the $L_1$ metric.

## Manhattan versus Euclidean length

The Euclidean distance $d_2 = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}$ is never larger than $d_1$, and the ratio $d_1/d_2$ ranges from 1 (a purely horizontal or vertical pair) to $\sqrt{2}$ (a 45-degree pair). For pins at $(10, 10)$ and $(40, 50)$ um, $d_1 = 30 + 40 = 70$ um while $d_2 = 50$ um, so the rectilinear wire is 20 um longer than the crow flies. This gap is why rectilinear Steiner trees, not Euclidean ones, are the right model for routed wirelength, and why some advanced nodes allow 45-degree routing on selected layers. A tool should never mix the two metrics silently: a placer that optimizes Euclidean distance while the router pays Manhattan distance is optimizing the wrong thing on diagonal nets.

## Many shortest paths

Between two points there is usually not one shortest rectilinear path but many. On a unit grid with no obstacles, a shortest path from $p$ to $q$ makes exactly $|\Delta x|$ horizontal and $|\Delta y|$ vertical steps, in any order, so the number of shortest paths is the binomial coefficient

$$\binom{|\Delta x| + |\Delta y|}{|\Delta x|}.$$

For $\Delta x = 4$ and $\Delta y = 3$ that is $\binom{7}{4} = 35$ routes of identical length. This freedom is what routers exploit: among equal-length paths they choose by congestion, via count or layer preference. It also explains why a maze router's search can explode on open areas and why routers prefer L- and Z-shaped patterns first: there are only two L-shapes, while the full set of shortest paths grows combinatorially.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters on global and detailed routing; de Berg, Cheong, van Kreveld and Overmars, "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (3rd ed., 2008), chapter 1.

label: Bounding boxes and rectangle intersection
lesson:
# Bounding boxes and rectangle intersection

The axis-parallel rectangle is the workhorse of layout geometry. Every shape has a bounding box, every spatial index stores boxes, and the first test in nearly every check is whether two boxes intersect. The operations are trivially cheap, a few comparisons, but they are executed billions of times in DRC, extraction and placement, and getting their edge cases right (touching versus overlapping, empty results) decides whether higher-level algorithms are correct.

## Boxes from points

The bounding box of a point set is $[\min x, \max x] \times [\min y, \max y]$. For a net's pins it gives the half-perimeter wirelength, $\text{HPWL} = (\max x - \min x) + (\max y - \min y)$, the standard placement estimate of routed length. It is exact for two- and three-pin nets (a rectilinear Steiner tree of three points has exactly that length) and a lower bound for larger nets. Example: pins $(3, 8)$, $(15, 2)$, $(9, 20)$ give a box from $x = 3$ to 15 and $y = 2$ to 20: HPWL $= 12 + 18 = 30$, area $12 \times 18 = 216$. The box can be updated incrementally when a pin moves, as long as the tool also tracks how many pins sit on each extreme, which is how placers keep HPWL current during millions of moves.

## Intersecting two rectangles

Two rectangles $A = [a_1, a_2] \times [b_1, b_2]$ and $B = [c_1, c_2] \times [d_1, d_2]$ intersect in the box whose x-range is $[\max(a_1, c_1), \min(a_2, c_2)]$ and likewise in y. The overlap lengths are

$$o_x = \min(a_2, c_2) - \max(a_1, c_1), \quad o_y = \min(b_2, d_2) - \max(b_1, d_1),$$

and the intersection area is $o_x o_y$ when both are positive, else 0. Example: $[2, 9] \times [1, 6]$ and $[5, 12] \times [4, 10]$ give $o_x = 9 - 5 = 4$, $o_y = 6 - 4 = 2$, area 8. The separation into independent x and y tests is the key structural fact: rectilinear intersection decomposes into one-dimensional interval problems, which is why sweeps and interval structures work so well here. The same two formulas, applied to grown boxes, answer distance questions, and applied to node bounding boxes, they drive every R-tree and bin-grid query in the engine.

## Edge cases and many rectangles

When $o_x = 0$ the rectangles touch along an edge; when both are 0 they touch at a corner. Whether touching counts as intersecting is a predicate choice: connectivity extraction must count shared edges as connected, while an overlap check for positive area must not. Each engine fixes the rule once and uses it everywhere. Intersection is associative, so the common region of several boxes is $[\max$ of left edges, $\min$ of right edges$]$ by the same in y. For $[0, 10] \times [0, 8]$, $[4, 14] \times [2, 12]$ and $[6, 9] \times [-3, 5]$, the common box is $[6, 9] \times [2, 5]$, area 9. The empty case appears as a negative extent, which code must test explicitly rather than multiplying two negatives into a positive area.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4 on wirelength estimation; the KLayout documentation on the Box class and DRC functions.

label: The orientation predicate
lesson:
# The orientation predicate

Almost every geometric algorithm, from convex hulls to polygon Booleans to segment intersection, branches on one question: given three points, do they make a left turn, a right turn, or lie on a line? The answer is the sign of a 2 by 2 determinant. It is the most frequently evaluated predicate in a geometry kernel, so its exactness and its cost shape the whole engine.

## The sign of a determinant

For points $a$, $b$, $c$ define

$$\text{orient}(a, b, c) = (b_x - a_x)(c_y - a_y) - (b_y - a_y)(c_x - a_x),$$

the z-component of the cross product of $b - a$ and $c - a$, and twice the signed area of triangle $abc$. It is positive when $a \to b \to c$ turns left (counter-clockwise), negative for a right turn and zero when the points are collinear. Example: $a = (1, 2)$, $b = (5, 3)$, $c = (2, 7)$ gives $(4)(5) - (1)(1) = 19 > 0$, a left turn. Everything else follows: a convex hull keeps left turns, a polygon's orientation is the sign of the sum of such terms, and a point is left of a directed edge when the orientation is positive. Because the value is an exact integer on integer input, the sign can be trusted completely when the arithmetic is wide enough.

## Deciding whether segments cross

Segments $pq$ and $rs$ properly cross exactly when $r$ and $s$ lie on opposite sides of line $pq$ and $p$ and $q$ lie on opposite sides of line $rs$:

$$\text{orient}(p, q, r) \cdot \text{orient}(p, q, s) < 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \text{orient}(r, s, p) \cdot \text{orient}(r, s, q) < 0.$$

Four predicate evaluations, no division and no intersection point. Example: $p = (0, 0)$, $q = (6, 6)$, $r = (0, 6)$, $s = (6, 0)$: the first pair gives $+36$ and -36, the second -36 and $+36$, so they cross. When any value is zero an endpoint is collinear with the other segment and the engine must handle touching and overlap explicitly. Computing the actual crossing point needs a division and is deferred until the topology is known.

## Exactness and bit width

With integer coordinates the predicate can be evaluated exactly, but only if the arithmetic is wide enough. If coordinates are signed $b$-bit integers, a difference needs $b + 1$ bits, so its magnitude is at most $2^b - 1$. Each product is at most $(2^b - 1)^2 < 2^{2b}$, and the determinant, twice the area of a triangle inside the coordinate square, is bounded by the same value. A signed type of $2b + 1$ bits therefore always suffices, and $2b$ bits do not. For 32-bit coordinates that is 65 bits, one more than a 64-bit integer. Engines respond by limiting the coordinate range, using 128-bit intermediates, or computing in floating point with an error bound and falling back to exact arithmetic only when the result is near zero.

## Going deeper

Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates" (Discrete and Computational Geometry, 1997); de Berg et al., "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (3rd ed., 2008), chapter 1.

label: Integer coordinates and exact predicates
lesson:
# Integer coordinates and exact predicates

A geometry engine for layout is only as trustworthy as its arithmetic. Layout data lives on an integer grid in database units, and the engine's decisions (is this point inside, do these edges cross, are these shapes touching) are signs of predicates. If a sign is computed wrongly the algorithm's decisions contradict each other and it produces garbage or crashes. This concept is about the representation choices that keep layout geometry exact and reproducible.

## Database units and the integer grid

A layout database stores every coordinate as an integer count of database units (DBU), for example 1 DBU = 1 nm. GDSII stores coordinates as 4-byte signed integers together with the unit size; OASIS uses variable-length integers. A coordinate of 12345 at 1 nm per DBU means 12.345 um. On top of the DBU grid the foundry imposes a manufacturing grid, say 5 nm, and every vertex must be a multiple of it. Integers make geometry exact: two edges are either at the same coordinate or not, areas are integers, and the same input always gives the same output. Converting to a finer DBU multiplies coordinates exactly; converting to a coarser one requires rounding and can move edges, so tools refuse or flag it.

## Exact predicates and overflow

Algorithms branch on predicate signs, such as the orientation determinant. In floating point the sign can be wrong when the true value is near zero, and then the algorithm can conclude both that a point is left of an edge and that it is right of it, producing broken polygons. With integer coordinates the predicate can be exact, but the arithmetic must be wide enough: with 32-bit coordinates a difference needs 33 bits and the determinant can need 65 bits. The standard engineering answer is a filtered predicate: evaluate quickly in floating point with a rigorous error bound, trust the sign when the value clears the bound, and recompute exactly in the rare uncertain cases. The result is exact and nearly as fast as the naive version.

## Where non-integer geometry sneaks in

Manhattan geometry is closed under Booleans: a vertical edge at $x = a$ meets a horizontal edge at $y = b$ exactly at $(a, b)$, so no new coordinates appear. Exactness breaks when non-axis edges enter. Two 45-degree or arbitrary-angle edges intersect at rational points that are generally off the grid, and sizing a diagonal edge by $d$ moves it by $d/\sqrt{2}$ in each axis. The engine must snap such points to the grid, and snapping perturbs edges: nearly coincident edges can collapse into zero-width slivers or start to cross. Transforms are another source: mirroring or rotating a cell about a half-unit coordinate maps integers to half-integers. Robust engines snap with care, then re-run the topology on the snapped result.

## Going deeper

Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates" (1997); Hobby, "Practical segment intersection with finite precision output" (Computational Geometry, 1999), on snap rounding; the Boost.Polygon documentation on its integer coordinate model.

label: Spacing between rectangles
lesson:
# Spacing between rectangles

Minimum spacing is the most common design rule: two shapes on a layer must be at least $s$ apart. The rule is stated as a distance, but a checker needs a formula for the distance between two rectangles, a choice of metric, and a way to avoid square roots. This concept computes rectangle-to-rectangle distance and shows how the metric changes the answer at corners, which is where most real spacing disputes happen.

## Facing edges

For rectangles $A$ and $B$ define the horizontal gap $g_x = \max(0, B.x_1 - A.x_2, A.x_1 - B.x_2)$ and the vertical gap $g_y$ likewise. If the x-projections overlap then $g_x = 0$, the shapes face each other across a horizontal or vertical channel, and the distance is simply the other gap. Example: $A = [0, 60] \times [0, 40]$ and $B = [85, 120] \times [10, 70]$ overlap in y, so the spacing is $g_x = 85 - 60 = 25$ nm. This is the common case in routed layouts, where parallel wires on a track grid face each other along their length. It is also where the parallel run length is measured, which more advanced spacing tables use. Most spacing violations in routed metal are of this facing kind, between neighbouring tracks.

## Corner to corner

When both gaps are positive, the closest points are two corners and the Euclidean distance is $\sqrt{g_x^2 + g_y^2}$. For $g_x = 30$ and $g_y = 40$ nm that is 50 nm, although neither gap alone is that large. Different metrics give different answers here: the square (Chebyshev) metric reports $\max(g_x, g_y) = 40$ nm, and a projection metric, which only measures shapes whose projections overlap, ignores the pair entirely. Foundry spacing rules are normally Euclidean, so corner-to-corner pairs need the full formula. Many DRC engines expose the metric as an option (Euclidean, square, projection), and choosing the wrong one either misses violations or floods the report with false ones at corners.

## Checking a rule without square roots

To test a rule $d \ge s$ the checker never takes a square root: it compares $g_x^2 + g_y^2$ with $s^2$ in exact integer arithmetic. A violation is $g_x^2 + g_y^2 < s^2$ for separated shapes. Example with $s = 50$: a neighbour with gaps $(0, 45)$ violates, $(30, 30)$ violates because $1800 < 2500$, and $(40, 35)$ passes because $2825 \ge 2500$. Shapes that overlap or touch merge into one polygon and are not spacing-checked against each other; they are handled by width and notch rules instead. The checker also needs a candidate set: only shapes within distance $s$ can violate, so a spatial query with the shape grown by $s$ finds the few neighbours worth testing.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula

A layout polygon is stored as a ring of integer vertices. Its area, needed for density, capacitance estimates, antenna ratios and fill, comes from the shoelace formula: a sum of cross products of consecutive vertices. The same sum also reveals orientation, which is how databases tell outer boundaries from holes. It is exact on integer data, linear time and the first thing to compute on any polygon.

## Summing cross terms

For a simple polygon with vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ listed in order,

$$A = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i),$$

with indices taken modulo $n$. Each term is twice the signed area of the triangle from the origin to an edge, and the triangles outside the polygon cancel. It is the discrete form of Green's theorem, $A = \frac{1}{2}\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx)$. Example: the L-shape $(0,0), (4,0), (4,2), (2,2), (2,5), (0,5)$ gives terms $0, 8, 4, 6, 10, 0$, sum 28, area 14, matching $4 \times 2 + 2 \times 3$. On integer coordinates the sum is an integer, so the area of a rectilinear polygon is computed exactly with no rounding at all. The cost is one multiply-and-subtract per vertex, so the area of every polygon in a layer comes out of a single linear pass.

## The sign gives orientation

The formula returns a signed area: positive when the vertices run counter-clockwise, negative when they run clockwise. A tool that stores outer boundaries counter-clockwise reads a negative result as a hole or as a ring that must be reversed. Reversing the vertex list flips the sign of every term. Example: listing the L-shape above as $(0,5), (2,5), (2,2), (4,2), (4,0), (0,0)$ gives -14. Orientation is not cosmetic. Boolean engines use it to decide which side of each edge is inside, fill rules depend on it, and two shapes with the same vertices but opposite orientation mean different things to an engine that counts winding. Normalizing orientation on input is one of the first steps of any geometry pipeline.

## Holes and multi-ring polygons

A polygon with holes is an outer ring plus inner rings, conventionally with opposite orientation: outer counter-clockwise, holes clockwise. Then the shoelace sum over all rings gives the net area directly, because each hole contributes its area with a negative sign. Example: an outer ring of area 60 with a clockwise $3 \times 2$ hole gives $60 - 6 = 54$. If a file stores every ring counter-clockwise, the tool must subtract hole areas explicitly. The same per-ring sum applies to perimeter (sum of edge lengths over all rings, holes included), which feeds sizing and fringe-capacitance estimates. Because the formula is linear in the rings, it also works incrementally: editing one ring changes only that ring's contribution.

# Point-in-polygon tests and fill rules

Deciding whether a point is inside a polygon underlies probing a net at a location, connectivity through vias, and the definition of what a self-overlapping or multi-ring shape even covers. The classic answer casts a ray and counts boundary crossings. For layout data the subtle part is the fill rule: even-odd and nonzero winding agree on simple polygons and disagree on overlapping ones, and the choice changes what a layer means.

## Counting ray crossings

Cast a ray from the query point, say towards $+x$, and count how many polygon edges it crosses. Each crossing switches between inside and outside, and the ray ends outside, so an odd count means the point is inside. For a rectilinear polygon only vertical edges can be crossed by a horizontal ray, and an edge at $x = e$ spanning $[y_1, y_2]$ is crossed when $e > q_x$ and $y_1 < q_y < y_2$. Example: a point at $(2.5, 3.5)$ with vertical edges to its right at $x = 4$ spanning $[0, 5]$ and at $x = 7$ spanning $[3, 8]$ crosses both, count 2, so it is outside. Degenerate cases, a ray through a vertex, are handled by a half-open rule such as counting an edge when $y_1 \le q_y < y_2$.

## Testing many points

Testing one point against an $n$-edge polygon costs $O(n)$. Testing $m$ points naively costs $O(mn)$, which is too slow for, say, probing every via against every shape. Two standard speed-ups apply. First, a bounding-box rejection test removes most points in $O(1)$. Second, sort the query points by y and sweep: the active edges at each y form an ordered list, and the crossing count for a point is its rank in that list, found by binary search. Example: with active vertical edges at $x = 1, 4, 7, 9$ on the query row, a point at $x = 5$ has two edges to its right and is outside, while a point at $x = 8$ has one and is inside. A slab or trapezoid structure gives $O(\log n)$ per query after preprocessing.

## Even-odd versus nonzero winding

When a boundary overlaps itself, or several rings overlap, parity and winding disagree. The winding number of a point counts how many times the boundary wraps around it, with counter-clockwise loops adding 1 and clockwise loops subtracting 1. Under the nonzero rule a point is inside when its winding number is not 0; under the even-odd rule, when its crossing count is odd. For a path drawn as several overlapping counter-clockwise rectangles, the winding number of a point equals the number of rectangles covering it. A point covered twice is inside under nonzero but outside under even-odd, which punches an accidental hole in the overlap. Layout semantics are normally a union, which corresponds to nonzero winding, so engines merge overlapping input before applying parity-based algorithms.

## Going deeper

# Boolean operations on layout polygons

DRC rule decks, derived layers, extraction and mask preparation are written as Boolean expressions over layers: gate = poly AND diffusion, contacts NOT covered by metal, the XOR of two versions of a layer. A Boolean engine takes two sets of polygons and returns the region in both, either, one but not the other, or exactly one. It is the core primitive of a layout geometry kernel, and its correctness is non-negotiable.

## AND as intersection

A AND B is the region covered by both layers. For two rectangles it is the intersection box computed from the overlaps of the x- and y-ranges, with area $o_x o_y$ when both overlaps are positive. Example: $A = [2, 10] \times [1, 7]$ and $B = [6, 14] \times [4, 12]$ give $[6, 10] \times [4, 7]$, area 12. For general polygons the engine sweeps both layers' edges together, tracking at each point how many shapes of each layer cover it, and emits the boundary where the coverage condition changes. AND is how derived layers are formed: a transistor gate region is poly AND active, and the gate length and width checks run on that derived layer.

## OR as union

A OR B is the region covered by at least one layer. Its area follows from inclusion-exclusion,

$$|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|,$$

so for the rectangles above, $48 + 64 - 12 = 100$. Union also merges: overlapping or touching input shapes on one layer become a single polygon, which is the normal first step before width, spacing and notch checks, because a spacing rule between two drawn rectangles that overlap is meaningless once they are one piece of metal. For many shapes, inclusion-exclusion explodes combinatorially, so engines compute unions by a sweep that maintains coverage counts, not by subtracting pairwise intersections.

## NOT and XOR

A NOT B (set difference) removes B's region from A: $|A \setminus B| = |A| - |A \cap B|$. A XOR B keeps what is in exactly one layer: $|A \oplus B| = |A| + |B| - 2|A \cap B|$. With the rectangles above, NOT gives $48 - 12 = 36$ and XOR gives $48 + 64 - 24 = 88$. NOT expresses enclosure and coverage rules: vias NOT covered by metal are violations. XOR is the comparison operator: two versions of a layout, or the outputs of two engines, should XOR to nothing, and the size and shape of a nonzero XOR tells exactly where they differ. All four operations are instances of one sweep with a different coverage predicate, which is how engines implement them.

## Going deeper

Vatti, "A generic solution to polygon clipping" (Communications of the ACM, 1992); the Boost.Polygon and KLayout documentation on Boolean operations; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on physical verification.

# Growing and shrinking polygons

Sizing moves every edge of a polygon outward (grow) or inward (shrink) by a distance $d$. It is how rule decks build halos and keep-outs, how bias is applied in mask preparation, and, combined with Booleans, how width and spacing checks are implemented. Morphologically, growing is a Minkowski sum with a square (or a disc) and shrinking is the corresponding erosion, so the results have exact geometric meaning.

## Sizing one rectangle

Growing a $w \times h$ rectangle by $d$ on every side gives $(w + 2d) \times (h + 2d)$; shrinking gives $(w - 2d) \times (h - 2d)$, and the rectangle disappears when either dimension is at most $2d$. Example: a $40 \times 26$ nm rectangle grown by 5 nm becomes $50 \times 36$, area 1800; shrunk by 5 nm it becomes $30 \times 16$, area 480; shrunk by 13 nm its height reaches 0 and it vanishes. Sizing rectilinear shapes with square corners keeps them rectilinear, which is why it is the default in layout tools. Growing is a Minkowski sum with a $2d \times 2d$ square centred at the origin, and shrinking is erosion by the same square. Engines treat the collapse as a removal, never as a negative rectangle.

## Sizing merges shapes

Grow two disjoint shapes and they merge when the gap between them is at most $2d$, because each side contributes $d$. That is the basis of spacing-by-sizing: grow each shape by $s/2$, and any separated pair closer than $s$ now overlaps. After growing, the union must be computed correctly. Example: $A = [0, 20] \times [0, 15]$ and $B = [26, 40] \times [5, 30]$ grown by 4 become $[-4, 24] \times [-4, 19]$ and $[22, 44] \times [1, 34]$; their overlap is $2 \times 18 = 36$, so the merged area is $28 \cdot 23 + 22 \cdot 33 - 36 = 1334$. Note that sizing a union differs from the union of sized shapes only in the overlap bookkeeping; the region itself is the same, because Minkowski sum distributes over union.

## Closing and opening

Growing then shrinking by the same $d$ is a closing: it fills gaps and notches narrower than $2d$ and otherwise returns the original shape. Shrinking then growing is an opening: it deletes parts narrower than $2d$ and restores the rest. They are not inverses. Example: two $h = 20$ bars with a 6 nm gap, closed with $d = 4$, become one bar spanning the gap, because the grown shapes fused and the bridge survives the shrink. With $d = 2$ the gap ($6 > 4$) never closes and the shapes return unchanged. Closing is used to merge nearly abutting shapes and detect notches; opening is the classic implementation of a minimum-width check, where whatever the opening removes is a width violation.

## Going deeper

Serra, "Image Analysis and Mathematical Morphology" (1982), on dilation, erosion, opening and closing; the KLayout DRC reference on sized, and on how width and space checks relate to sizing.

label: Area after offsetting a rectilinear polygon
prereqs: Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula
lesson:
# Area after offsetting a rectilinear polygon

Fill engines, keep-out generators and density estimators need the area of a grown or shrunk polygon without always building it. For rectilinear polygons there is an exact closed form in terms of area, perimeter and corner counts, valid as long as the offset does not make distant parts of the shape interact. It turns sizing into arithmetic, and the conditions under which it breaks are exactly the conditions under which sizing changes topology.

## The A plus P d plus 4 d squared law

Grow a rectilinear polygon with area $A$ and perimeter $P$ by $d$ with square corners. Each edge of length $\ell$ sweeps an outward strip of area $\ell d$. Each convex corner adds a $d \times d$ square; at each reflex corner two strips overlap in a $d \times d$ square that was counted twice. A rectilinear polygon always has exactly 4 more convex than reflex corners, so

$$A_{\text{grown}} = A + P d + 4 d^2.$$

Shrinking by $d$ gives $A - P d + 4 d^2$ by the mirror argument, provided no part is narrower than $2d$. Example: a polygon with $A = 120$, $P = 52$ grown by 2 has area $120 + 104 + 16 = 240$. A $10 \times 6$ rectangle checks the law: $(14)(10) = 140 = 60 + 32 \cdot 2 + 16$. The law needs only two numbers per polygon, so a fill or keep-out estimator can predict grown areas without building any geometry.

## Applying it to a vertex list

Given vertices, compute $A$ by the shoelace formula and $P$ as the sum of edge lengths $|\Delta x| + |\Delta y|$, then apply the law. Example: the polygon $(0,0), (5,0), (5,2), (9,2), (9,7), (0,7)$ has area $5 \cdot 7 + 4 \cdot 5 = 55$ and perimeter $5 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 9 + 7 = 32$; grown by 1 it covers $55 + 32 + 4 = 91$. The law needs the offset not to make separate parts meet. Outward, that means no pocket of the exterior is narrower than $2d$: inside a narrower notch the two wall strips overlap and the law overcounts. Inward, no neck or arm may be narrower than $2d$. These are exactly the cases where a closing or opening would change the shape, and an engine should check them rather than trust the formula.

## Round corners and the Euclidean offset

A Euclidean offset adds every point within distance $d$ of the polygon. Edges still sweep strips of area $\ell d$ and reflex corners still remove a $d \times d$ overlap, but each convex corner now adds a quarter disc of area $\pi d^2/4$ instead of a square. With $c$ convex and $r$ reflex corners ($c = r + 4$),

$$A_{\text{grown}} = A + P d + \left(\frac{\pi c}{4} - r\right) d^2.$$

For a convex polygon this is $A + Pd + \pi d^2$, the classical Steiner formula. Example: $A = 55$, $P = 32$, $r = 1$, $c = 5$, $d = 1$ gives $55 + 32 + 3.927 - 1 = 89.93$. The law also needs every edge next to a reflex corner to be at least $d$ long, or a quarter disc spills into a neighbouring strip.

## Going deeper

Santalo, "Integral Geometry and Geometric Probability" (1976), on Steiner's formula for parallel bodies; the KLayout documentation on sizing modes and corner handling.

label: Minkowski sums and keep-out regions
lesson:
# Minkowski sums and keep-out regions

The Minkowski sum $A \oplus B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}$ is the operation behind sizing, keep-out regions and configuration spaces. Growing a shape by $d$ is its sum with a square or disc. The set of positions where a via centre would violate spacing to an obstacle is a sum of the obstacle with the via's shape. Knowing how sums behave for rectangles and convex polygons turns these questions into arithmetic.

## Sums of rectangles

For axis-parallel rectangles the sum is again a rectangle whose ranges are the sums of the ranges:

$$[a_1, a_2] \times [b_1, b_2] \oplus [c_1, c_2] \times [d_1, d_2] = [a_1 + c_1, a_2 + c_2] \times [b_1 + d_1, b_2 + d_2].$$

Widths and heights add. Example: $[3, 9] \times [2, 6]$ plus $[-2, 1] \times [0, 5]$ is $[1, 10] \times [2, 11]$, area 81. Sizing by $d$ is the special case $B = [-d, d]^2$, which adds $2d$ to each dimension. Because the Minkowski sum distributes over union, $(A_1 \cup A_2) \oplus B = (A_1 \oplus B) \cup (A_2 \oplus B)$, a rectilinear polygon decomposed into rectangles can be grown by growing each rectangle and taking the union. This is also why sizing a union of rectangles never needs anything more than per-rectangle arithmetic followed by one union, a pattern that grow-based checks rely on throughout the rule deck.

## Convex sums and edge directions

For convex polygons $P$ and $Q$, the boundary of $P \oplus Q$ is obtained by merging their edges sorted by direction, like merging two sorted lists. Edges with the same outward normal fuse into one longer edge. So with $m$ and $n$ edges and $k$ shared normal directions, the sum has $m + n - k$ edges, and it is computed in $O(m + n)$ time. Example: a rectangle (normals 0, 90, 180, 270 degrees) plus an octagon with all eight 45-degree normals shares 4 directions, so the sum has $4 + 8 - 4 = 8$ edges. This is why growing an octagonal via by a square keeps it an octagon, and why sums of non-convex shapes, which can have quadratic complexity, are computed by decomposing into convex pieces first.

## Configuration space for placement

Ask where the centre of a via may go without violating spacing $s$ to an obstacle. Shrink the via to its centre point and expand the obstacle by the via's half-dimensions plus the spacing: the forbidden region is the obstacle summed with the via shape reflected through its centre and grown by $s$. For an obstacle $w \times h$, a via $a \times b$ and square-metric spacing $s$, the forbidden region is $(w + a + 2s) \times (h + b + 2s)$. Example: obstacle $200 \times 120$ nm, via $40 \times 40$ nm, $s = 50$ nm gives $340 \times 260$ nm. Legal positions are the complement, so detailed routers and legalizers test a single point against grown obstacles instead of testing two shapes against each other.

## Going deeper

de Berg et al., "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (3rd ed., 2008), chapter 13 on robot motion planning and Minkowski sums; Lozano-Perez, "Spatial planning: a configuration space approach" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1983).

label: Polygon representations in layout databases
prereqs: Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula
lesson:
# Polygon representations in layout databases

The same region can be stored as a vertex ring, a set of oriented edges, a stack of trapezoids, a bitmap or a hierarchy of placed cells. Each representation makes some operations cheap and others expensive, and a geometry engine converts between them constantly: rings for storage and area, edges for Booleans, trapezoids for mask writing, hierarchy for repetition. Knowing what each one preserves is how a tool designer decides where an operation should run.

## Vertex rings and their orientation

The canonical storage form is a ring of integer vertices with an orientation convention: outer boundaries counter-clockwise, holes clockwise. A ring gives area and perimeter in one pass and is compact. For Manhattan polygons each step changes only x or only y, so storing alternating coordinates halves the data. Rings should be normalized: no consecutive collinear vertices, no repeated points, a fixed starting vertex. Then two tools that produce the same region produce the same ring, which makes comparison and hashing trivial. The weakness is that rings say nothing about how shapes relate to each other: overlaps between rings, or a ring that touches itself, are invisible until an algorithm looks for them.

## Edge sets, trapezoids and scanlines

Boolean engines break rings into oriented edges, each carrying a direction that says which side is inside. A sweep over all edges, counting coverage, evaluates any Boolean expression for any number of overlapping shapes, and output edges are chained back into rings at the end. A scanline (trapezoid) form cuts each region into bands between consecutive vertex y-values, each band a list of x-intervals; clipping and Booleans become interval operations, and mask writers consume trapezoids directly as exposure figures. A bitmap makes coverage and density trivial but quantizes edges to the pixel size. The trade-off is always the same: the form that makes one operation linear makes reconstruction of another expensive.

## Holes, cut lines and file formats

GDSII stores a boundary as one vertex list with no notion of holes, so a ring-shaped region is written with a cut line: a zero-width slit from the outer boundary to the hole and back (the keyhole). A reader must merge the polygon before checking it, or the slit looks like two edges at zero spacing. OASIS adds rectangle and trapezoid records, repetitions for arrays and modal values that avoid restating shared fields, with variable-length integers, so regular structures compress dramatically. Above shapes sits hierarchy: a cell stored once and placed many times, with transforms. An engine that works on hierarchy directly processes each cell once and only revisits instances where their surroundings interact.

## Going deeper

The SEMI P39 OASIS specification; the Calma GDSII Stream Format manual; the KLayout documentation on polygon and edge classes.

label: The plane-sweep paradigm
lesson:
# The plane-sweep paradigm

A plane sweep turns a two-dimensional problem into a sequence of one-dimensional ones. A vertical line moves across the plane, stopping only at events (shape edges, endpoints, intersections), while a status structure holds the objects the line currently cuts. Union area, overlap reporting, segment intersection, Boolean operations and connectivity extraction in layout tools are all sweeps. The paradigm is why these problems cost $O(n \log n)$ plus output, not $O(n^2)$.

## Events and stops

For rectangles, the events are their left and right edges: $2n$ events for $n$ rectangles, sorted by x in $O(n \log n)$. Nothing changes between consecutive event x-values, so the sweep only needs to stop at distinct event coordinates, processing all events at one x together. Example: rectangles $[0, 5] \times \cdot$, $[3, 9] \times \cdot$ and $[5, 12] \times \cdot$ have six events at x-values $0, 3, 5, 5, 9, 12$, so five stops. The order of events at the same x is a design decision with consequences: processing removals before insertions makes touching shapes non-overlapping, and the reverse makes them overlap. Engines choose the order to match the predicate they implement.

## The status structure

Between stops, the status holds the objects the sweep line cuts, ordered along the line, typically in a balanced search tree keyed by y. At a left edge the rectangle is inserted; at a right edge it is deleted; each update costs $O(\log m)$ for $m$ active objects. The maximum status size is the depth of the deepest overlap of x-ranges, which for layout data is usually far smaller than $n$: a vertical line across a chip cuts only the shapes in one column. Example: x-ranges $[0, 6]$, $[2, 8]$, $[4, 10]$, $[7, 12]$ are three deep at $x = 5$ and never four deep, so the status never holds more than three rectangles. Memory for a sweep is proportional to that peak, not to the whole layout.

## Why the sweep is fast

A sweep only compares objects that are in the status at the same time, which means their x-ranges overlap. Pairs whose x-ranges are disjoint are never compared at all. Brute force tests all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs; the sweep tests only x-overlapping pairs and, with a good status structure, only those that also come close in y. Example: six rectangles have 15 pairs, but if only 5 of them overlap in x, the sweep hands just those 5 to the y-test. The total cost becomes $O(n \log n)$ for sorting and status updates plus $O(k)$ or $O(k \log n)$ for the $k$ reported results, an output-sensitive bound. This locality is what makes full-chip checks tractable.

## Going deeper

Bentley and Ottmann, "Algorithms for reporting and counting geometric intersections" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1979); de Berg et al., "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (3rd ed., 2008), chapter 2.

label: Line-segment intersection by sweep
lesson:
# Line-segment intersection by sweep

Finding all crossings among wire segments is the textbook sweep problem and a direct layout need: crossings on the same layer are shorts, and crossings between layers are where vias may go and where coupling is computed. For Manhattan segments the sweep is especially simple; for general segments the Bentley-Ottmann algorithm finds all $k$ crossings among $n$ segments in $O((n + k) \log n)$ time.

## Crossings of horizontal and vertical segments

A horizontal segment from $(x_1, y)$ to $(x_2, y)$ and a vertical segment from $(x, y_1)$ to $(x, y_2)$ cross when $x_1 < x < x_2$ and $y_1 < y < y_2$, a pair of interval tests. Example: H from $(0, 3)$ to $(8, 3)$ and V from $(5, 0)$ to $(5, 6)$ cross at $(5, 3)$; V from $(9, 0)$ to $(9, 6)$ does not, since 9 is outside $[0, 8]$. Testing every pair costs $O(n_h n_v)$. Whether endpoints touching a segment count as crossings is again a predicate choice; for shorts detection on merged polygons touching is connectivity, while for crossing counts it is usually excluded. Manhattan crossings always lie on existing coordinates, so the computation is exact. On a large layer the pair loop is far too slow, which is what the sweep below fixes.

## The orthogonal sweep

Sweep left to right. Events are the endpoints of horizontal segments and the x-positions of vertical segments. Insert a horizontal segment into a tree keyed by y at its left endpoint and delete it at its right endpoint. At a vertical segment, run a one-dimensional range query on the tree for y in $[y_1, y_2]$, reporting every active horizontal it crosses. Example: at a vertical segment at $x = 5$, three horizontals may be active (their x-ranges contain 5), and a range query over the vertical's span reports the two whose y lies inside it. Each query costs $O(\log n + k_v)$, so the whole algorithm runs in $O(n \log n + k)$, which is optimal for reporting.

## Bentley-Ottmann and output sensitivity

For segments at arbitrary angles, the status is the list of segments ordered by their y at the sweep line, and that order changes exactly at crossings. Bentley-Ottmann keeps an event queue of endpoints and of crossings between status neighbours, discovered on the fly; only adjacent segments can cross next. Each of the $2n + k$ events costs $O(\log n)$, giving $O((n + k)\log n)$. Compare brute force at $n(n-1)/2$ pair tests. With $n = 2^{16}$ and $k = n$, brute force does about $2.1 \times 10^9$ tests while the sweep does about $2.1 \times 10^6$ operations, a thousand times fewer. When $k$ approaches $n^2$ the advantage disappears, but layout data is sparse: most segments cross few others.

label: Area of a union of rectangles by sweep
lesson:
# Area of a union of rectangles by sweep

The area covered by overlapping rectangles, counting overlaps once, is needed for density checks, fill targets and capacitance estimates on unmerged data. Inclusion-exclusion over many shapes is hopeless, but a sweep solves it in $O(n \log n)$: the area is the integral over x of the covered length of the sweep line. The same machinery, with counts instead of flags, measures area covered at least $k$ times.

## Slabs and covered length

Sort the distinct x-coordinates of all rectangle edges. Between consecutive ones, the set of rectangles cut by the sweep line is constant, so the covered region within that slab is (slab width) times (covered length of the line). The union area is the sum over slabs:

$$A = \sum_i (x_{i+1} - x_i)\, L(x_i).$$

Example: $[0, 4] \times [0, 3]$ and $[2, 6] \times [1, 5]$. Slab $[0, 2]$ has covered length 3, slab $[2, 4]$ has the union of $[0, 3]$ and $[1, 5]$, length 5, and slab $[4, 6]$ has length 4. Total $6 + 10 + 8 = 24 = 12 + 16 - 4$, agreeing with inclusion-exclusion. This is the discrete form of integrating covered length over x. The number of slabs is at most $2n - 1$, so the work is dominated by computing each slab's covered length quickly.

## Maintaining the covered length

At each stop, the status must report $L$, the length of the union of active y-intervals, under insertions and deletions. Recomputing it from scratch costs $O(n)$ per stop and $O(n^2)$ overall. A segment tree over the compressed y-coordinates stores in each node a cover count (how many active intervals cover the node's whole range) and the covered length within the node: the full range if the count is positive, otherwise the sum of the children. Each insertion or deletion touches $O(\log n)$ nodes, and $L$ is read at the root. Example: active y-ranges $[0, 3]$, $[1, 5]$ and $[7, 9]$ merge into $[0, 5]$ and $[7, 9]$, so $L = 7$.

## Area covered at least twice

Replace the covered flag by a cover count and the same sweep measures the area covered by at least $k$ rectangles: in each slab, sum the lengths where the count is at least $k$. With $k = 2$ this finds double coverage, which matters for checks such as overlapping fill, double-patterning conflicts and duplicated geometry. Example: three rectangles pairwise overlapping in regions of area 4, 6 and 2, with a common triple region of area 1, cover $4 + 6 + 2 - 2 \cdot 1 = 10$ at least twice. Inclusion-exclusion needs every intersection; the sweep needs only counts. A segment tree supports this by storing, per node, the length covered at least once and at least twice.

## Going deeper

Bentley, "Algorithms for Klee's rectangle problems" (Carnegie Mellon University report, 1977); de Berg et al., "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (3rd ed., 2008), chapter 10 on segment trees.

label: Reporting overlapping rectangle pairs
lesson:
# Reporting overlapping rectangle pairs

Many checks begin by finding every pair of shapes that overlap, or that come closer than a rule distance: shorts between nets, spacing candidates, enclosure pairs. Reporting all $k$ such pairs among $n$ rectangles takes $O(n \log n + k)$ with a sweep, and the same algorithm, run on grown shapes, finds near pairs. The predicate details (overlap, touch, closer than $s$) decide what the report means.

## Overlap means both projections overlap

Two rectangles overlap with positive area exactly when their x-ranges overlap with positive length and their y-ranges do too. A sweep in x keeps active rectangles in an interval structure on y; when a rectangle is inserted, a query for intervals overlapping its y-range reports every active rectangle that overlaps it. Each pair is reported once, when the later-starting rectangle enters. Example: $[0, 6] \times [0, 4]$, $[4, 9] \times [2, 7]$ and $[7, 12] \times [0, 3]$: the first two overlap ($2 \times 2$), the last two overlap ($2 \times 1$), and the first and third have disjoint x-ranges, so 2 pairs. With an interval tree as the status, the cost is $O(n \log n + k)$.

## Near pairs by growing

To find separated pairs closer than $s$ in the square metric, where distance is $\max(g_x, g_y)$, grow every rectangle by $s/2$ and report overlaps: two shapes closer than $s$ in both axes have grown versions that overlap. Pairs that already touched or overlapped before growing are excluded, since they merge. Example with $s = 4$: shapes with gaps $(3, 0)$ and $(2, 3)$ are flagged, a shape with gaps $(5, 1)$ is not, because its x-gap alone reaches the rule. For a Euclidean rule the grown-overlap report is a superset, and each candidate is then confirmed with $g_x^2 + g_y^2 < s^2$. This filter-then-refine pattern is the general structure of distance queries.

## Touching is a separate predicate

Two closed rectangles touch when their overlaps in x and y are both at least 0 but not both positive: they share an edge segment or a corner. Touching pairs have zero overlap area, so an area-overlap report misses them, yet they matter: shapes that share an edge are electrically connected after merging, and a corner-only touch is a classic ambiguous case that design rules often forbid. Example: $[0, 3] \times [0, 3]$ and $[3, 5] \times [1, 4]$ share the edge from $(3, 1)$ to $(3, 3)$; $[0, 3] \times [0, 3]$ and $[3, 6] \times [3, 6]$ touch at one corner. An engine must define, once, whether its overlap predicate uses closed or open intervals, and apply that choice consistently in sweeps, indexes and Booleans.

## Going deeper

label: Point location by slabs and trapezoidal maps
lesson:
# Point location by slabs and trapezoidal maps

Point location asks which region of a planar subdivision contains a query point: which polygon a probe lands on, which net a via hits, which tile of a partition a coordinate falls in. With preprocessing, queries take $O(\log n)$. The slab method shows the idea simply but can need quadratic storage; the trapezoidal map achieves linear size and logarithmic expected query time and is the structure behind many practical locators.

## Slabs from vertical lines

Draw a vertical line through every segment endpoint. Within each slab between consecutive lines, no segment starts or ends, so the segments crossing the slab are totally ordered from bottom to top. With $m$ distinct endpoint x-values there are $m + 1$ slabs, counting the two unbounded ones. A query does two binary searches: one over the slab boundaries to find the slab, one over the slab's ordered segments using orientation tests to find the segment just below the point. Example: segments with endpoints at $x = 2, 5, 5, 9, 11, 14$ have five distinct x-values and six slabs. Both searches are $O(\log n)$, so queries are fast, and the structure is simple to build with a sweep.

## The cost of slabs

Each slab stores its own sorted list of the segments spanning it. A long segment spans many slabs and is stored in every one. Total storage is the sum over slabs of the number of spanning segments, which can reach $\Theta(n^2)$: picture $n/2$ long horizontal segments stacked over $n/2$ short ones that create $n$ slab boundaries. Example: with boundaries at $x = 0, 4, 6, 10$ and segments covering $[0, 10]$, $[0, 6]$ and $[4, 10]$, the three bounded slabs hold $2 + 3 + 2 = 7$ entries for three segments. Persistent search trees cut storage to $O(n)$ by sharing structure between consecutive slabs, which differ by only a few insertions and deletions, an elegant result that motivates the alternative below.

## Trapezoidal maps

A trapezoidal map shoots vertical extensions from each endpoint only up and down to the nearest segment, instead of across the whole plane. Inside a bounding box, $n$ non-crossing segments produce at most $3n + 1$ trapezoids and at most $6n + 4$ vertices, so the map has linear size. Built by randomized incremental insertion, with a search structure (a directed acyclic graph of x-tests and segment tests) recording the history, it takes $O(n \log n)$ expected time and answers queries in $O(\log n)$ expected time. Example: 100 segments give at most 301 trapezoids. The same decomposition into trapezoids is used by Boolean engines and mask fracturers, so the structure doubles as a geometric representation.

## Going deeper

label: Interval trees
lesson:
# Interval trees

An interval tree stores $n$ intervals and answers stabbing queries, all intervals containing a point, in $O(\log n + k)$ time with $O(n)$ storage. It is the one-dimensional workhorse behind sweep statuses, cut-line queries in routers, and the y-dimension of rectangle overlap reporting. The centred version is short to describe and shows clearly why the query never wastes work.

## Stabbing queries

Given closed intervals $[a_i, b_i]$ and a query $q$, the stabbing query reports every interval with $a_i \le q \le b_i$. In layout this is: which wires cross the cut line $y = q$, which rows a coordinate falls in, which shapes are active at a sweep position. Example: intervals $[2, 9]$, $[5, 14]$, $[10, 18]$, $[12, 20]$ and query 12 report $[5, 14]$, $[10, 18]$, $[12, 20]$, three intervals, since 12 lies in $[12, 20]$ as a closed endpoint. A linear scan costs $O(n)$ per query; an interval tree pays $O(n \log n)$ once to build and then answers each query in time proportional to $\log n$ plus the answer size, which matters when there are millions of queries. The query is also the core operation of a sweep status, where the stabbing point is the current sweep position.

## Building a centred interval tree

Choose a centre $x_c$, typically the median of all endpoints. Intervals containing $x_c$ are stored at the root; intervals entirely left of $x_c$ go to the left subtree and those entirely right go to the right subtree, recursively. The root keeps its intervals in two lists, sorted by left endpoint ascending and by right endpoint descending. Because the median splits the endpoints evenly, the depth is $O(\log n)$, and every interval is stored exactly once, so storage is $O(n)$. Example: with centre 15, $[10, 18]$ and $[12, 20]$ stay at the root, $[2, 9]$ goes left, and $[16, 25]$ goes right. Intervals are never split, unlike in a segment tree.

## Querying the root

Every interval at the root contains $x_c$. If the query $q$ is left of $x_c$, a root interval contains $q$ exactly when its left endpoint is at most $q$, because its right endpoint is already beyond $x_c > q$. So scan the list sorted by left endpoint and stop at the first left endpoint greater than $q$. Symmetrically, for $q > x_c$ scan by right endpoint descending and stop at the first right endpoint less than $q$. Then recurse into one child only. Example: root centre 15 with $[10, 18]$, $[12, 20]$, $[14, 16]$ and $q = 13$: left endpoints 10, 12, 14, so two are reported and the scan stops at 14. Each node costs $O(1 + k_{\text{node}})$, and the path has $O(\log n)$ nodes.

prereqs: Area of a union of rectangles by sweep
lesson:
# Segment trees and canonical decomposition

A segment tree stores intervals by splitting each into $O(\log n)$ canonical pieces that are nodes of a balanced tree over the elementary intervals. It uses $O(n \log n)$ storage but supports what interval trees cannot easily do: aggregates over coverage, such as the covered length used by the union-area sweep, and multi-level structures for rectangle queries. Understanding canonical decomposition is the key to using it.

## Elementary intervals

Sort the distinct endpoints $p_1 < \dots < p_m$ of all intervals. They cut the line into elementary intervals: the open gaps $(p_i, p_{i+1})$, the single points $[p_i, p_i]$ and the two unbounded ends, $2m + 1$ pieces in all. Within one elementary interval every input interval either covers all of it or none of it, so the elementary intervals are the leaves of the tree. Example: intervals $[2, 7]$, $[4, 9]$, $[7, 12]$ have distinct endpoints 2, 4, 7, 9, 12, so $m = 5$ and there are 11 leaves. In integer layout coordinates many tools simplify to half-open unit cells $[i, i + 1)$ between compressed coordinates, which removes the point leaves. The tree over these leaves is built bottom-up in linear time once the endpoints are sorted.

## Canonical nodes

Each tree node covers the union of its leaves. An interval is stored at its canonical nodes: the highest nodes whose range lies entirely inside the interval and whose parent's range does not. Descend from the root; at a node fully inside the interval, store it and stop; at a node disjoint from it, stop; otherwise recurse into both children. At most two nodes per level are stored, so each interval uses $O(\log n)$ nodes. Example: over 8 unit leaves $[0, 8)$, the interval $[1, 7)$ decomposes into $[1, 2)$, $[2, 4)$, $[4, 6)$ and $[6, 7)$, four canonical nodes. A stabbing query walks one root-to-leaf path and reports every interval stored on it, in $O(\log n + k)$.

## Storage and aggregates

Summing canonical nodes over all intervals gives the storage, $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case, against $O(n)$ for an interval tree. The payoff is that each node's stored set is a clean unit for aggregates. The union-area sweep stores at each node a count of intervals covering it fully and the covered length below it: if the count is positive the covered length is the node's whole range, otherwise the sum of its children's. An insertion or deletion updates only the $O(\log n)$ canonical nodes and their ancestors. Example: over 16 leaves, intervals $[0, 16)$, $[3, 5)$ and $[2, 11)$ need 1, 2 and 4 entries, 7 in all. Multi-level segment trees, with a second structure at each node, answer rectangle queries in $O(\log^2 n + k)$.

## Going deeper

label: R-trees for spatial queries
lesson:
# R-trees for spatial queries

The R-tree is the standard dynamic index for rectangles: a height-balanced tree whose nodes store the minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs) of their children. Window queries descend only into children whose MBR meets the window. It handles insertions and deletions, works for shapes of any size, and is the index behind many layout databases and spatial databases. Its performance depends entirely on how much node MBRs overlap.

## Node bounding rectangles

A leaf stores entries (shape id plus bounding box); an internal node stores, for each child, the MBR of everything below it. The MBR of a set of boxes is $[\min x_1, \max x_2] \times [\min y_1, \max y_2]$. Every node holds between $m$ and $M$ entries (the root excepted), and all leaves sit at the same depth, so the height is $O(\log_m n)$. Example: entries $[3, 6] \times [4, 7]$, $[5, 9] \times [2, 5]$ and $[4, 8] \times [6, 10]$ give the MBR $[3, 9] \times [2, 10]$, area 48, although the entries cover far less. That empty area inside MBRs is the dead space that makes queries visit nodes containing nothing relevant.

## Descending into children

A window query starts at the root and descends into every child whose MBR intersects the window, pruning the others together with their whole subtrees. At the leaves it tests each entry and reports those that intersect. Example: a root with children MBRs $[2, 16] \times [3, 17]$, $[23, 37] \times [5, 19]$ and $[11, 25] \times [23, 37]$ and a window $[14, 22] \times [10, 20]$ descends only into the first child: the second starts at $x = 23$, beyond the window, and the third starts at $y = 23$. Unlike a k-d tree's cells, R-tree MBRs may overlap, so a query point can lie in several children and all of them must be searched; there is no worst-case logarithmic bound for window queries.

## Counting the work of a query

The cost of a query is the number of rectangle tests: every entry of every visited node. For a two-level tree that is the number of root entries plus the entries of each child that is visited. Example: a root with 3 children, of which 2 meet the window and hold 4 and 3 entries, costs $3 + 4 + 3 = 10$ tests, and perhaps 2 entries are reported. A brute-force scan of the 11 entries would cost 11 tests; the saving grows with depth and data size, since each level prunes most of the tree. Query cost rises with node overlap and dead space, which is why split policies and bulk loading, which control the shape of MBRs, decide R-tree quality.

label: R-tree node splitting
lesson:
# R-tree node splitting

When an R-tree node overflows, its entries must be divided between two nodes, and the division decides how much the resulting MBRs overlap and how much dead space they enclose. Every later query pays for a poor split. Guttman's quadratic split and the R*-tree's criteria of overlap and margin are the classic policies, and both are simple area and perimeter computations on boxes.

## Dead area of a pair

Guttman's quadratic split measures how badly two entries fit together by the dead area they would waste in a shared node:

$$d(E_1, E_2) = \text{area}(\text{MBR}(E_1 \cup E_2)) - \text{area}(E_1) - \text{area}(E_2).$$

Example: $E_1 = [0, 3] \times [0, 2]$ and $E_2 = [8, 10] \times [5, 9]$ have a joint MBR $[0, 10] \times [0, 9]$ of area 90, so $d = 90 - 6 - 8 = 76$, a lot of empty space. Two nearby boxes give a small $d$; overlapping boxes can make $d$ negative, since their overlap is subtracted twice. The quantity is cheap to compute and captures the intuition that entries far apart should not share a node. Because it depends only on the two boxes, it can be computed for every pair before any assignment decision is made.

## Picking seeds

PickSeeds evaluates $d$ for every pair of the $M + 1$ entries and takes the pair with the largest dead area as the seeds of the two new nodes: they are the worst pair to keep together. The remaining entries are then assigned one at a time, each to the node whose MBR it enlarges least, choosing first the entry with the strongest preference. The seed step costs $O(M^2)$, hence the name quadratic; a linear variant picks seeds by the largest normalized separation along each axis. Example: among four entries, scoring the six pairs and finding the maximum $d = 76$ for the far-apart pair makes those two the seeds, and the other entries join whichever seed is closer in enlargement.

## Overlap and margin in the R*-tree

The R*-tree evaluates candidate splits more carefully. For each axis it sorts entries by their lower and upper coordinates and considers every split into two groups of allowed sizes. It picks the split axis by the smallest sum of margins (the perimeters of the two group MBRs), which favours square-ish nodes, and then the split by the smallest overlap area between the two group MBRs, breaking ties by total area. Example: groups with MBRs $[2, 9] \times [1, 6]$ and $[7, 15] \times [4, 12]$ have margins 24 and 32, sum 56, and overlap $2 \times 2 = 4$. Overlap matters most: a query falling in the overlap must descend into both nodes. The R*-tree also reinserts some entries on overflow, which improves the tree further.

## Going deeper

label: k-d trees and nearest neighbors
lesson:
# k-d trees and nearest neighbors

A k-d tree splits space recursively, alternating axes, at the median of the points: x at the root, y at the next level, and so on. It answers range queries and nearest-neighbour queries over points, such as cell centres, pin locations or legal sites, by pruning cells that cannot contain an answer. It is static by nature but cheap to build in $O(n \log n)$ and very fast on point data.

## Splitting at the median

To build a 2-d tree, sort the points by x and split at the median: the median point is stored at the root, points with smaller x go left and larger x go right. Each child then splits its own points at their median y, and the axes alternate down the tree. Splitting at the median keeps the tree balanced with depth $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$. Example: points with x-coordinates $3, 8, 12, 17, 21, 26, 30$ split at $x = 17$, the fourth of seven. Presorting by both coordinates, or using linear-time selection, gives $O(n \log n)$ construction. The tree partitions the plane into rectangular cells, one per leaf, with no overlap, unlike an R-tree.

## Alternating axes

At depth one the splitting coordinate switches to y. Each child takes only its own points and splits them at their median y. Example: if the three points left of the root have y-values 5, 19, 33, the left child splits at $y = 19$; the right child splits its own points independently, at a different y. The resulting cells adapt to the data: dense regions get small cells and empty regions large ones. For range queries on $n$ points in two dimensions the k-d tree visits $O(\sqrt{n} + k)$ nodes in the worst case, since a query boundary line can cross only $O(\sqrt{n})$ cells. Alternating axes is the simplest rule; splitting along the axis of largest spread often works better on skewed data.

## Pruning a nearest-neighbour search

To find the nearest point to a query $q$, descend to the leaf cell containing $q$ and take the best candidate there, at distance $r$. Then unwind: a cell must be searched only if its distance from $q$ is less than $r$, because nothing inside it can be closer otherwise. In the Manhattan metric the distance from $q$ to a cell is its x-gap plus its y-gap, zero if $q$ is inside. Example: with $r = 6$, a cell 4 units to the right and 3 units above $q$ is at L1 distance 7 and is pruned, while a cell 2 to the right with an overlapping y-range is at distance 2 and is searched. Every improved candidate shrinks $r$ and prunes more, which gives about $O(\log n)$ expected time on well-distributed data.

label: Quadtrees over the die
lesson:
# Quadtrees over the die

A quadtree recursively divides a square region into four equal quadrants, stopping where a cell is simple enough: empty, or holding few objects. Over a die of side $W = 2^k$ the cell sizes are powers of two, so every cell index is a bit-shift of a coordinate. Quadtrees index points, rectangles and rasterized layers, and the same hierarchy underlies multi-resolution density maps and hierarchical routing grids.

## Cell size by depth

At depth $d$ (the root at depth 0) a quadtree over a $W \times W$ die has cells of side $W / 2^d$, and there are $4^d$ of them if the tree is complete. To get cells no larger than a target size $s$, the depth must satisfy $W / 2^d \le s$, so $d = \lceil \log_2 (W/s) \rceil$. Example: a die of 4096 units with features of 100 units needs $d = 6$, because $4096/32 = 128 > 100$ while $4096/64 = 64 \le 100$. In practice quadtrees are adaptive: only cells that contain too many objects subdivide, so empty regions stay coarse. That makes them compact on clustered layouts where a uniform grid would waste memory on empty bins.

## Separating two points

In a point-region quadtree, a cell subdivides until each point has its own cell. At depth $d$ the cell index of a point is $(\lfloor x / c \rfloor, \lfloor y / c \rfloor)$ with $c = W/2^d$; two points share a cell until those indices first differ. With $W = 2^k$, the index is the top $d$ bits of each coordinate, so the separation depth is set by the first leading bit in which $x$ or $y$ differ. Example: in $[0, 256)$, points $(100, 40)$ and $(110, 45)$ share cells while $c \ge 16$, since $\lfloor 100/16 \rfloor = \lfloor 110/16 \rfloor = 6$, and separate at $c = 8$, depth 5, where $12 \ne 13$. Close points force deep trees, which is why point quadtrees limit depth or store several points per leaf.

## Rectangles across cells

A rectangle stored in a quadtree either goes into the smallest cell that contains it entirely (the MX-CIF scheme) or is registered in every cell it overlaps at a chosen depth. For half-open cells of side $c$ and a rectangle $[x_1, x_2) \times [y_1, y_2)$, the overlapped columns run from $\lfloor x_1/c \rfloor$ to $\lfloor (x_2 - 1)/c \rfloor$ and similarly for rows. Example: cells of side 32 and the rectangle $[20, 75) \times [64, 70)$ span columns 0 to 2 and row 2 only, so 3 cells. Storing in every overlapped cell duplicates large shapes; storing in the smallest enclosing cell avoids duplication but puts shapes that straddle a major boundary near the root, where every query meets them.

## Going deeper

Samet, "Foundations of Multidimensional and Metric Data Structures" (2006), chapters 1 and 3; Finkel and Bentley, "Quad trees: a data structure for retrieval on composite keys" (Acta Informatica, 1974).

lesson:
# Uniform grids and bins

The simplest spatial index divides the die into equal bins and keeps, for each bin, the shapes that overlap it. Lookup is arithmetic, insertion and deletion are trivial, and on evenly spread layout data it is hard to beat. Placers, routers and DRC engines all use bin grids. Their weaknesses, duplicated large shapes and uneven bin loads, are equally simple to quantify.

## Bin index arithmetic

With square bins of side $b$, $C$ columns and $R$ rows, the bin holding point $(x, y)$ has column $\lfloor x/b \rfloor$ and row $\lfloor y/b \rfloor$, and in row-major numbering its index is $\text{row} \cdot C + \text{col}$. Bins are half-open so that every point belongs to exactly one bin. Example: bins of 50 nm, 12 columns, point $(437, 268)$: column 8, row 5, index $5 \cdot 12 + 8 = 68$. No tree descent, no comparisons beyond two divisions; with $b$ a power of two the divisions become shifts. This is why global placers and routers use grids of bins for density and congestion: the bin of every cell or wire segment is known in constant time.

## Shapes in several bins

A rectangle is registered in every bin it overlaps. With half-open coordinates its columns run from $\lfloor x_1/b \rfloor$ to $\lfloor (x_2 - 1)/b \rfloor$ and its rows likewise, and it occupies (columns) times (rows) bins. Example: with $b = 25$ the shape $[40, 90) \times [10, 30)$ spans columns 1 to 3 and rows 0 to 1, six bins. Total storage is the sum over shapes, so a few long wires or large blocks can dominate memory. A query that collects shapes from several bins sees a long shape more than once and must de-duplicate, for example by reporting a pair only from the bin containing a reference corner of their intersection. Choosing $b$ near the typical shape size keeps duplication low.

## Expected candidates per query

If $n$ small shapes are spread uniformly over $C \times R$ bins, each bin holds $n/(CR)$ shapes on average, and a query window touching $q$ bins fetches about $q n/(CR)$ candidates, which are then tested exactly. Example: 50,000 shapes over $10 \times 10$ bins and a query touching 4 bins: $4 \cdot 500 = 2000$ candidates. Making bins smaller reduces candidates per query but increases duplication and the number of bins a query touches; the sweet spot keeps a constant number of shapes per bin. The average hides the weakness: layouts are clustered, so some bins hold thousands of shapes while others are empty, and hierarchical structures such as quadtrees and R-trees adapt where a grid cannot.

## Going deeper

Samet, "Foundations of Multidimensional and Metric Data Structures" (2006), chapter 1; the OpenROAD documentation for its global placer and global router, which use bin grids for density and congestion.

label: Choosing a spatial index
lesson:
# Choosing a spatial index

Interval trees, segment trees, R-trees, k-d trees, quadtrees, bin grids and bounding volume hierarchies all answer "what is near here", but each is tuned to a different query, data shape and update pattern. Choosing well is a design decision that sets the cost of every check and every move in the engine. This concept is about matching structure to workload, and about why hierarchy and spatial locality make full-chip checking tractable at all.

## Matching the query to the structure

Name the query first. A stabbing query on intervals (which wires cross a cut line) is an interval tree. A window query over boxes (which shapes lie near this rectangle) is an R-tree or a bin grid, and a distance query becomes a window query once the window is grown by the distance. A nearest-neighbour query over points (the nearest legal site, the closest pin) is a k-d tree or, for a regular site array, plain arithmetic. An aggregate over coverage (covered length at a sweep stop) is a segment tree. A bounding volume hierarchy, a tree of nested boxes built top-down, serves the same queries as an R-tree when objects are known in advance. The wrong match still works but pays a large factor.

## Static versus dynamic data

Some workloads load data once and query it many times (batch DRC on a finished layout); others interleave updates and queries (an incremental router, a placer's legalizer, an interactive editor). Static workloads favour structures built in bulk: a k-d tree split at medians, or an R-tree bulk-loaded by sorting along a space-filling curve or by tiling, giving tight, barely overlapping nodes. Dynamic workloads favour structures with cheap local updates: bin grids and R-trees. R-trees stay height-balanced under updates, but their MBRs bloat and overlap over time, so query cost creeps up; R*-tree reinsertion or periodic rebuilding restores it. A k-d tree degrades under updates because its splits no longer match the data.

## Hierarchy and why DRC stays tractable

Two facts keep checking a billion shapes feasible. First, rules have a small interaction distance, so each shape needs comparing only with nearby shapes, found by a sweep or a spatial index; the work is near-linear instead of quadratic. Second, layouts are hierarchical: a cell stored once and placed thousands of times can be checked once, and only its interaction region, the band within the rule distance of other geometry, needs checking in each context. Hierarchical engines therefore index cell bounding boxes as well as shapes and flatten selectively where instances overlap heavily. When a design has little repetition, the bookkeeping of hierarchy costs more than it saves, and flat processing with good spatial indexing wins.

## Going deeper

prereqs: Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula
lesson:
# Convex hulls by monotone chain

The convex hull of a point set is the smallest convex polygon containing it. Layout tools use hulls for blockage and keep-out outlines, for quick containment and separation tests, as a building block of Voronoi and Delaunay computations, and as a lower bound in packing and floorplanning. Andrew's monotone chain computes it in $O(n \log n)$ with nothing but sorting and the orientation predicate, and it is the version to implement.

## Hull vertices

A hull vertex is an extreme point: it cannot be written as a convex combination of the others. Points strictly inside, and points lying on a hull edge between two corners, are not vertices. The hull of $n$ points has $h \le n$ vertices, and for points on a small lattice many points are collinear, so a careful implementation must decide whether to keep collinear boundary points; layout outlines normally drop them. Example: the points $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(4, 4)$, $(0, 4)$, $(2, 2)$, $(2, 0)$ have a hull of four vertices: $(2, 2)$ is inside and $(2, 0)$ lies on the bottom edge. The hull of rectangles is the hull of their corners, since a convex set containing all corners contains every rectangle.

## Andrew's monotone chain

Sort the points by x, breaking ties by y. Build the lower hull left to right: append each point, but first pop the last point while the last two kept points and the new one fail to make a strict left turn, that is, while their orientation is at most 0. Build the upper hull the same way from right to left. Concatenate the two chains, dropping the duplicated endpoints. Each point is pushed once and popped at most once, so after the $O(n \log n)$ sort the scan is linear. Example: sorted points $(0, 0)$, $(1, 2)$, $(2, 1)$, $(3, 0)$: after $(2, 1)$ arrives, $(1, 2)$ is popped (a right turn), and after $(3, 0)$ arrives, $(2, 1)$ is popped, leaving the lower hull $(0, 0)$, $(3, 0)$ with two points.

## Area and the lower bound

Once the hull is a counter-clockwise ring, its area comes from the shoelace formula; for integer points it is a multiple of $\frac{1}{2}$. Example: the hull $(0, 0)$, $(6, 0)$, $(7, 3)$, $(2, 5)$ has shoelace sum $0 + 18 + 29 + 0 = 47$, area 23.5. The $O(n \log n)$ cost is optimal for comparison-based algorithms: sorting can be reduced to hull construction by lifting numbers $x_i$ onto the parabola $(x_i, x_i^2)$, whose hull lists them in order. Output-sensitive algorithms (Chan's, $O(n \log h)$) win when the hull is small. For rectilinear layout outlines, the orthogonal hull, the smallest region convex along every horizontal and vertical line, is often more useful than the convex hull and is computed by a similar sweep.

## Going deeper

label: Voronoi diagrams
lesson:
# Voronoi diagrams

The Voronoi diagram of a set of sites divides the plane into cells, each holding the points closer to one site than to any other. It answers nearest-site questions in one structure and appears in layout as the basis of critical-area analysis for yield (how far a defect must reach to short two wires), of proximity and clearance computation, and of meshing. Its size is linear in the number of sites, which follows from Euler's formula.

## Linear size from Euler's formula

The Voronoi diagram of $n$ sites, not all collinear, is a planar subdivision: vertices are points equidistant from three or more sites, edges are pieces of perpendicular bisectors. Every vertex has degree at least 3. Adding a vertex at infinity to close the unbounded edges and applying Euler's formula $V - E + F = 2$ with $F = n$ cells gives at most $2n - 5$ vertices and at most $3n - 6$ edges. Example: 100 sites produce at most 195 Voronoi vertices and 294 edges. So the diagram has linear size, and Fortune's sweep-line algorithm builds it in $O(n \log n)$, optimal because sorting reduces to it. A diagram of quadratic size would be useless for a billion-shape layout; a linear one is practical.

## Unbounded cells and the hull

A site's cell is unbounded exactly when the site lies on the boundary of the convex hull of all sites. For a hull site there is a direction in which it stays the nearest site forever; an interior site is surrounded on all sides. So the number of unbounded cells equals the number of sites on the hull, $h$, which for points in general position is the number of hull vertices. Example: sites $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(5, 9)$, $(4, 3)$, $(6, 2)$ have hull vertices $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(5, 9)$, so three cells are unbounded and two are bounded. The unbounded edges, $h$ of them, are the bisectors of consecutive hull vertices, which is how a hull computation seeds a Voronoi construction.

## Exact counts and metrics

In general position (no four sites on a circle), every Voronoi vertex has degree exactly 3 and the bounds become exact counts in terms of $n$ and the number $h$ of hull sites: $2n - 2 - h$ vertices and $3n - 3 - h$ edges, matching the triangles and edges of the dual Delaunay triangulation. Example: 50 sites with 8 on the hull give 90 vertices and 139 edges. Layout often needs other metrics. Under the $L_\infty$ or $L_1$ metric, bisectors are polygonal lines with horizontal, vertical and 45-degree pieces, which suits rectilinear geometry. Voronoi diagrams of segments, not points, give the medial axis of shapes and clearance between wires, the basis of critical-area extraction for shorts and opens.

## Going deeper

Aurenhammer, "Voronoi diagrams: a survey of a fundamental geometric data structure" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991); Fortune, "A sweepline algorithm for Voronoi diagrams" (Algorithmica, 1987); Papadopoulou and Lee, "Critical area computation via Voronoi diagrams" (IEEE TCAD, 1999).

label: Delaunay triangulation
lesson:
# Delaunay triangulation

The Delaunay triangulation connects sites whose Voronoi cells share an edge. It is the triangulation that avoids skinny triangles where it can: it maximizes the minimum angle over all triangulations. That makes it the standard mesh for field solvers and finite-element models in extraction and thermal analysis. Its counts follow from Euler's formula, and its defining test, the empty circle, is a single determinant.

## Counting triangles and edges

Any triangulation of $n$ points in the plane, $h$ of them on the convex hull, has exactly $2n - 2 - h$ triangles and $3n - 3 - h$ edges. Euler's formula gives it: with $V = n$ and $F = T + 1$ faces counting the outer one, each triangle has 3 edges and each edge borders two faces, except the $h$ hull edges, so $3T + h = 2E$. Example: 40 points with 6 on the hull give 72 triangles and 111 edges, whether the triangulation is Delaunay or not. The Delaunay triangulation is the dual of the Voronoi diagram: one triangle per Voronoi vertex and one edge per Voronoi edge, which is why the counts match. Building it takes $O(n \log n)$ by divide and conquer or by randomized incremental insertion.

## The incircle test

A triangulation is Delaunay when no point lies strictly inside the circumcircle of any triangle. For a counter-clockwise triangle $abc$ and a point $d$, the test is the sign of

$$\det \begin{pmatrix} a_x - d_x & a_y - d_y & (a_x - d_x)^2 + (a_y - d_y)^2 \\ b_x - d_x & b_y - d_y & (b_x - d_x)^2 + (b_y - d_y)^2 \\ c_x - d_x & c_y - d_y & (c_x - d_x)^2 + (c_y - d_y)^2 \end{pmatrix},$$

positive when $d$ is inside, negative outside, zero on the circle. It is the orientation test lifted onto the paraboloid $z = x^2 + y^2$. Example: $a = (0, 0)$, $b = (4, 0)$, $c = (0, 4)$ and $d = (1, 1)$ give a determinant of 96, so $d$ is inside. Like orientation, it must be evaluated exactly, and on integer input it needs roughly twice the bits of the orientation test. Incremental Delaunay algorithms call it once per candidate edge flip, so its cost and exactness dominate their robustness.

## Refining a mesh

Field solvers refine meshes by inserting Steiner points where triangles are too large or too skinny. Inserting a point strictly inside the hull leaves the hull unchanged, so by the counting formula each insertion adds 2 triangles and 3 edges; locally, the new point splits its triangle into three, and edge flips driven by the incircle test restore the Delaunay property. Example: a mesh of 200 points with 12 on the hull has 386 triangles; adding 30 interior points gives 446. Mesh size drives solver cost, since the linear system has one unknown per node, so quality-driven refinement (Ruppert's algorithm, Chew's algorithm) that bounds angles while adding few points directly sets extraction run time and accuracy.

## Going deeper
