label: Decomposing rectilinear polygons into rectangles
prereqs: Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula
lesson:
# Decomposing rectilinear polygons into rectangles

Many consumers of layout geometry want rectangles, not polygons: mask writers, some extractors, fill generators, simple DRC engines and data compressors. Partitioning a rectilinear polygon into the fewest non-overlapping rectangles is solvable exactly in polynomial time, by a beautiful reduction to bipartite matching. Covering with overlapping rectangles, by contrast, is NP-hard, which is why tools partition.

## Reflex vertices

A vertex of a rectilinear polygon is convex (interior angle 90 degrees) or reflex (270 degrees). Walking the boundary counter-clockwise, every left turn is convex and every right turn reflex, and the turns must total one full rotation, so convex minus reflex equals 4. A simple rectilinear polygon with $n$ vertices therefore has $r = (n - 4)/2$ reflex vertices. Example: an L-shape has 6 vertices and 1 reflex vertex; a plus shape has 12 vertices and 4 reflex vertices. In a polygon with holes, each hole's corners count from the region's point of view: a rectangular hole contributes 4 reflex vertices. Reflex vertices are where any rectangle partition must place a cut, since no rectangle can have a 270-degree corner.

## Chords and the r minus g plus 1 formula

Every reflex vertex needs at least one cut. A single axis-parallel cut from a reflex vertex resolves one reflex vertex and adds one rectangle, giving $r + 1$ rectangles. A chord, an axis-parallel segment through the interior joining two reflex vertices, resolves two at once. The minimum partition of a simple rectilinear polygon has

$$r - g + 1$$

rectangles, where $g$ is the largest number of chords that pairwise do not intersect, not even at endpoints. Horizontal chords never cross each other, nor do vertical ones, so the chord intersection graph is bipartite, and its maximum independent set is the number of chords minus a maximum matching (Konig's theorem). Example: a plus shape has $r = 4$ and four chords forming a cycle; $g = 2$, so 3 rectangles. A T-shape has $r = 2$, one chord, and 2 rectangles; a U-shape has no chord and needs 3.

## Holes and degenerate cases

With $h$ holes the minimum becomes $r - g - h + 1$, where $r$ counts reflex vertices on all rings. Example: a square frame (one rectangular hole) has $r = 4$ and no chords, so $4 - 0 - 1 + 1 = 4$ rectangles, the four sides. A rectangle with two holes side by side at the same height has $r = 8$ and two chords between the holes, so $8 - 2 - 2 + 1 = 5$. The algorithm cuts along the chosen chords, then resolves each remaining reflex vertex with one cut, all in polynomial time. Collinear chains of reflex vertices and degenerate holes need care, and they are where implementations break. The contrast matters for tool design: the minimum cover, with overlaps allowed, is NP-hard, so mask and fill tools partition, and sometimes accept more pieces in exchange for speed.

## Going deeper

label: Slab decomposition versus minimum partition
lesson:
# Slab decomposition versus minimum partition

The simplest way to cut a rectilinear polygon into rectangles is to slice it with horizontal lines from every reflex vertex: a sweep produces it directly, it is easy to make robust, and mask fracturers and trapezoid-based Boolean engines use it. It is not minimal. Knowing how far it is from the minimum, and when a vertical slicing does better, is the practical side of rectangle decomposition.

## Horizontal slabs

Extend a horizontal cut from every reflex vertex into the interior until it meets the boundary. Between consecutive vertex y-values the polygon is a set of horizontal runs, and runs with the same x-extent in consecutive bands that are not separated by a cut stack into one rectangle. A sweep from bottom to top produces the pieces directly: start a rectangle when a run appears or changes, end it when the run ends or changes. Example: an H-shape (two posts joined by a crossbar) gives five rectangles: the two posts are cut above and below the crossbar, and the crossbar band is one full-width piece. A U-shape gives three, the same as the minimum. Each reflex vertex adds at most one cut, so at most $r + 1$ pieces without holes.

## The gap to the minimum

Slab cuts resolve each reflex vertex separately and ignore chords, especially vertical ones, so slabs can use far more rectangles than the minimum $r - g - h + 1$. Example: the H-shape has $r = 4$ and two vertical chords along the crossbar's sides; the minimum is $4 - 2 + 1 = 3$ (two posts and the crossbar), while slabs give 5. A comb with $t$ teeth on a vertical spine gives $2t - 1$ slabs against a minimum of $t + 1$. For mask writing the extra pieces cost write time, and for extraction or fill they cost memory and run time. The slab result is still valuable: it is canonical (unique for a given polygon), trivial to verify, and compatible with sweep-based engines.

## Choosing the slicing direction

Slicing vertically instead (cuts up and down from every reflex vertex) gives a different count, and a tool can compute both and keep the better. Example: the H-shape sliced vertically gives the two posts and the crossbar, 3 rectangles, which here equals the minimum, while horizontal slicing gives 5. A comb with teeth to the right of a vertical spine behaves the same way. For a plus shape both directions give 3. Some shapes defeat both directions, needing a mix of horizontal and vertical cuts, which is exactly what the matching-based minimum finds. Production fracturers add more criteria than count: they avoid slivers narrower than the writer's minimum figure size, prefer cuts on existing edges and keep runs aligned between neighbouring polygons.

## Going deeper

label: Spacing checks over many shapes
lesson:
# Spacing checks over many shapes

A full spacing check finds every pair of separated shapes on a layer closer than the rule, across billions of shapes, and with rules that depend on widths, run lengths and corners. It combines everything before it: rectangle distance, the choice of metric, sweeps or spatial indexes to find candidates, and table lookups for advanced rules. This is the check that dominates DRC run time and most violation reports.

## Pairwise Euclidean violations

For separated shapes $A$ and $B$ with gaps $g_x$ and $g_y$, a Euclidean spacing rule $s$ is violated when $g_x^2 + g_y^2 < s^2$. Touching or overlapping shapes are merged first and never spacing-checked against each other. The checker avoids testing all $n(n - 1)/2$ pairs: it grows each shape by $s$ (or $s/2$ each) and uses a sweep or spatial index to find only the pairs that come within the rule, then evaluates the exact test on those candidates. Example: among six shapes with rule 5, perhaps 15 pairs exist but only 4 come within 5 units in both axes, and 3 of those fail the Euclidean test. The output is a set of markers, usually the region between the offending edges, for each violation.

## Square versus Euclidean metrics

The square metric, $\max(g_x, g_y)$, is cheaper (no squaring) and never larger than the Euclidean distance, so it flags every Euclidean violation plus some corner-to-corner pairs that actually pass. A pair with gaps $(3, 3)$ under rule 4 is flagged by the square metric (3 < 4) but passes the Euclidean rule ($\sqrt{18} \approx 4.24 \ge 4$). Projection metrics only measure pairs whose edges face each other, so they miss corner pairs entirely. Engines therefore use the cheap metric as a filter and the Euclidean metric for sign-off, or expose the metric per rule, because some foundry rules are written for projection only (for example, end-of-line and parallel-run rules) while basic spacing is Euclidean.

## Width and run-length dependent spacing

At advanced nodes the required spacing depends on context. A spacing table, like the LEF SPACINGTABLE PARALLELRUNLENGTH construct, indexes the requirement by the wider wire's width and by the parallel run length, the overlap of the two wires' projections along their length. Example table: for widths above 0, 150 and 400 nm and run lengths above 0, 200 and 500 nm, requirements of 70, 70, 70 / 70, 90, 110 / 70, 120, 160 nm. Two wires of widths 180 and 90 nm running in parallel for 320 nm use the row for width above 150 and the column above 200: 90 nm. The checker must therefore compute widths (which needs the merged polygon) and run lengths for each candidate pair before it knows the threshold to compare against.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference, section on SPACINGTABLE; the KLayout DRC reference on space, separation and metrics; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on physical verification.

label: Width checks by shrinking and regrowing
lesson:
# Width checks by shrinking and regrowing

A minimum-width rule says no part of a shape may be narrower than $w$. Width is not a property of a rectangle but of every neck and arm of a merged polygon, which makes it harder than it sounds. Morphology gives a clean implementation: an opening (shrink then grow by $w/2$) removes exactly the parts too narrow to hold a $w \times w$ square, and the removed area marks the violations. The same sizing trick, with AND, implements spacing.

## Opening removes narrow shapes

Shrink a shape by $d$ and then grow the result by $d$. A rectangle with both sides greater than $2d$ shrinks to a smaller rectangle and grows back exactly; one with a side below $2d$ vanishes in the shrink and nothing grows back. So for isolated rectangles the area lost to an opening by $d$ is the total area of those narrower than $2d$, and those are exactly the width violations for a rule of $2d$. Example: with $d = 3$, rectangles of $10 \times 4$, $8 \times 9$ and $5 \times 12$ lose the first and third (4 and 5 are below 6), area $40 + 60 = 100$. Engines then XOR the original with the opened result to produce violation markers. A side of exactly $2d$ is the boundary case, which the engine's open or closed convention decides.

## Narrow arms of one polygon

For a merged polygon, the opening keeps every point that some $2d \times 2d$ square inside the polygon covers. A thick body survives whole, while an arm narrower than $2d$ cannot hold the square anywhere, not even straddling the junction, because the square would stick out of the arm; so the arm disappears and leaves the body. An arm wider than $2d$ survives entirely. Example: a $20 \times 16$ body with a $12 \times 3$ arm, opened with $d = 2$: the arm is 3 wide, below 4, so it vanishes, and the area left is 320. This is why width must be checked on merged polygons: two overlapping drawn rectangles can each be wide while their union has a narrow neck, or each be narrow while their union is wide.

## Spacing by growing and AND

To find spacing violations with rule $s$, grow every shape by $s/2$ and AND shapes from different polygons: a separated pair with gap $g < s$ now overlaps. For two shapes facing each other across an x-gap $g$, with y-ranges overlapping by $L$, the grown shapes overlap by $s - g$ in x and by $L + s$ in y (each y-range grew by $s/2$ at both ends), so the AND has area $(s - g)(L + s)$. Example: $s = 20$, $g = 12$, $L = 30$ gives an $8 \times 50$ marker of area 400. Growing with square corners checks the square metric; a Euclidean check either grows with rounded corners or confirms corner candidates exactly. The marker's size is not the violation's size, so tools report the facing edges as well.

## Going deeper

Serra, "Image Analysis and Mathematical Morphology" (1982); the KLayout DRC reference on width, space and sized.

prereqs: Area of a union of rectangles by sweep
lesson:
# Density windows and fill

Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material unevenly unless every region of every layer has similar metal density. Foundries therefore require density between a minimum and a maximum in every window of a given size, and fill tools insert dummy metal to meet the minimum. The computation is a union area clipped to windows, repeated over a sliding grid of windows, which makes efficient area accounting the core of a density engine.

## Density of one window

The density of a window is the area of metal inside it divided by the window area. Shapes must be clipped to the window, and overlapping shapes must be merged, or overlaps are counted twice. Example: a $50 \times 50$ um window containing $[0, 20] \times [0, 10]$, $[10, 30] \times [5, 25]$ and $[40, 60] \times [40, 55]$: clip the third to $[40, 50] \times [40, 50]$ (area 100); the first two have areas 200 and 400 with overlap $10 \times 5 = 50$, so the union is 550. Total 650 out of 2500, density 26.0 percent. Clipping is an AND with the window and merging is an OR, so density is a Boolean expression plus an area, and a union-area sweep computes it.

## Fill to reach a minimum

If a window's density is below the minimum $D$, fill must add at least $D \cdot A_w - A_m$ of area, where $A_w$ is the window area and $A_m$ the existing metal. With fill squares of side $f$ that never overlap existing metal, the count is $\lceil (D A_w - A_m)/f^2 \rceil$. Example: a $100 \times 100$ um window with 1500 square um of metal and a 25 percent minimum needs $2500 - 1500 = 1000$ square um, so 63 squares of $4 \times 4$ um. Real fill must also respect spacing to signal wires, the maximum density, and coupling capacitance on critical nets, so the fill engine's job is a constrained placement problem whose feasibility depends on the free space, which is itself a Boolean NOT of the existing layer grown by the fill spacing.

## Sliding windows

Density rules apply to every position of a window sliding over the die with a given step, not to a fixed tiling. A $w \times w$ window stepping by $t$ over a $W \times W$ die takes $(W - w)/t + 1$ positions per axis, so $((W - w)/t + 1)^2$ windows. Example: a 100 um window stepping 50 um over a 2000 um die gives 39 per axis, 1521 windows. Computing each window's area from scratch would repeat work, so engines precompute the metal area per step-sized tile once (a union-area sweep per tile) and sum tiles for each window, with a two-dimensional prefix sum making every window an $O(1)$ lookup. A smaller step catches more local density extremes but multiplies the windows.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Robins, Singh and Zelikovsky, "Filling algorithms and analyses for layout density control" (IEEE TCAD, 1999); the OpenROAD documentation for its density fill tool.

prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Hierarchical layout and flat shape counts

A chip layout is a hierarchy: standard cells placed in blocks, blocks in the top level, memories as arrays of bit cells. Stored hierarchically it is compact; flattened, a modern design has billions of shapes. Hierarchical processing exploits repetition by doing work once per cell, and the question that decides whether it pays is which instances interact with their surroundings. Counting shapes and interactions makes the trade-off concrete.

## Flattening by multiplication

The hierarchy is a directed acyclic graph: each cell holds its own shapes and instances of other cells. The flat shape count of a cell is its own shapes plus, for each child placement, the child's flat count. Computing bottom-up, each cell once, gives the total by the product rule. Example: cell C has 40 shapes; B has 10 shapes and 6 instances of C, so $10 + 240 = 250$; A has 20 shapes, 4 instances of B and 2 of C, so $20 + 1000 + 80 = 1100$; the top has 5 shapes and 100 instances of A, so $110{,}005$ flat shapes. Counts multiply down the hierarchy, which is how a few thousand distinct cells become billions of shapes, and why flattening is the expensive step to avoid.

## What hierarchy saves

A hierarchical engine stores and checks each cell's own shapes once, not once per placement. The saving is the ratio of flat shapes to shapes stored once per cell. Example: in the hierarchy above, the cells store $40 + 10 + 20 + 5 = 75$ shapes, against 110,005 flat, a ratio of about 1466.7. The saving is real only for work that does not depend on context. A cell's internal width and spacing results are the same everywhere, but anything near its boundary depends on what is placed next to it. Hierarchical DRC engines therefore check each cell in isolation, then check interaction regions per context, and promote or flatten geometry where contexts differ too much for reuse to pay.

## Interaction between instances

Two instances interact when geometry from one comes within the rule's interaction distance of the other; then their shared border must be checked together. For a row of $k$ instances of width $w$ at pitch $p$, instances $i$ and $j$ have bounding boxes $(j - i)p - w$ apart, and they must be checked together when that gap is below the interaction distance $s$. Example: $k = 8$, $w = 100$, $p = 120$, $s = 50$: adjacent instances are 20 apart and interact, instances two apart are 140 apart and do not, so 7 pairs. Abutted standard cells interact with every neighbour, so the interaction regions are a thin band along each row. That band, not the cell interiors, is where hierarchical checking spends its effort.

## Going deeper

The KLayout documentation on deep (hierarchical) mode; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on physical verification.

# Overlap area and parallel run length

Parasitic extraction turns geometry into capacitance and resistance. Its geometric inputs are simple: the overlap area between shapes on different layers (plate capacitance), the parallel run length and spacing between neighbouring wires on one layer (coupling capacitance), and the widths and lengths of wires (resistance). Rule-based extractors compute these quantities with Booleans and sweeps, then look up capacitance per unit from precharacterized tables.

## Parallel run length

Two parallel horizontal wires couple along the length where their x-projections overlap, the parallel run length (PRL):

$$\text{PRL} = \max(0, \min(a_2, b_2) - \max(a_1, b_1)).$$

Example: wires over $x \in [40, 300]$ and $x \in [120, 450]$ have a PRL of $300 - 120 = 180$ nm. The coupling capacitance between them is roughly proportional to PRL divided by a function of their spacing, so an extractor needs both numbers for every neighbouring pair. Wires that do not overlap in projection have PRL 0 and couple only weakly through fringe fields at their ends. PRL also enters design rules: the spacing table at advanced nodes requires more space for long parallel runs, so the same quantity serves both DRC and extraction.

## Overlap between layers

Where a wire on metal 1 crosses a wire on metal 2, the overlap area forms a parallel-plate capacitor through the dielectric between them. The total overlap area between two layers is the area of their AND, which for rectangular wires is the sum of pairwise intersection areas (when shapes on each layer are already merged and disjoint). Example: M1 wires $[0, 50] \times [0, 4]$ and $[5, 60] \times [20, 26]$ crossing an M2 wire $[10, 16] \times [0, 40]$ overlap it in $6 \times 4 = 24$ and $6 \times 6 = 36$, total 60. Plate capacitance is that area times a per-unit-area coefficient for the layer pair, plus fringe terms per unit perimeter of the overlap. A sweep or spatial index finds the crossing pairs without testing every combination.

## Neighbours within a coupling window

Coupling falls off quickly with distance, so extractors consider only neighbours within a window $S$ of the victim wire, and often only the nearest neighbour on each side along each stretch (the others are shielded). For each neighbour with edge-to-edge gap at most $S$, the extractor adds its PRL with the victim, usually binned by spacing so that each bin uses its own capacitance per unit length. Example: a victim over $x \in [0, 200]$ with neighbours at gaps 15, 40 and 22 nm and PRLs 120, 90 and 60 nm, with $S = 30$, counts $120 + 60 = 180$ nm. The search is a window query: grow the victim by $S$ and ask the index for shapes on the same layer.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on timing closure and parasitics; the OpenROAD documentation for OpenRCX.

label: Connectivity extraction with union-find
lesson:
# Connectivity extraction with union-find

Layout-versus-schematic and every net-aware check start by deciding which shapes are electrically connected: shapes that overlap or abut on a layer, joined across layers by vias and contacts. The result is a set of nets, the connected components of a graph whose vertices are shapes. Building that graph needs geometric overlap queries; computing components needs a disjoint-set (union-find) structure, which processes the overlaps in near-linear time.

## Components on one layer

On one layer, two shapes are connected when they overlap or share a boundary segment of positive length; touching only at a corner is ambiguous and is usually treated as not connected (and often flagged by a rule). The nets are the connected components of the graph with an edge for every connected pair. Example: shapes $[0, 4] \times [0, 2]$, $[4, 6] \times [0, 5]$, $[10, 12] \times [0, 3]$ and $[6, 8] \times [5, 7]$: the first two share an edge, the second and fourth touch only at the corner $(6, 5)$, and the third is alone, so there are 3 nets. A sweep that reports touching and overlapping pairs produces the edges, and union-find merges them without ever building the graph explicitly.

## Across layers through vias

Connectivity across layers is defined by the process: a via on the via layer connects the metal shapes above and below that it overlaps. The extractor finds, for each via, the M1 shapes and M2 shapes it overlaps (two window queries), and unions them. A via that lands on only one layer connects nothing and is often a violation in itself. Example: three M1 wires and three M2 wires form six shapes; two vias each join one M1 wire to one M2 wire, merging six components into four nets. Stacked vias, contacts to diffusion and poly, and wells extend the same idea through the whole layer stack, defined by a connectivity table in the rule deck. The result labels every shape with a net id.

## Union-find in practice

A disjoint-set forest keeps each component as a tree with a representative root. Union links two roots; find walks to the root, compressing the path on the way. With union by rank or size and path compression, a sequence of $m$ operations on $n$ elements costs $O(m\,\alpha(n))$, where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any realistic $n$. A union call merges only when its two shapes are in different sets, so the number of successful merges is $n$ minus the number of components. Example: 8 shapes with union calls (1, 2), (3, 4), (2, 1), (2, 3), (5, 6) merge 4 times, since (2, 1) repeats a connection, leaving 4 nets. Incremental extraction keeps the forest and updates it as edits arrive, though deletions require rebuilding affected components.

## Going deeper

Tarjan, "Efficiency of a good but not linear set union algorithm" (Journal of the ACM, 1975); the KLayout documentation on LVS and net tracing; Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), chapter on disjoint sets.

label: The geometry kernel as a protected core
prereqs: Core versus change surface per engine
lesson:
# The geometry kernel as a protected core

Every DRC, extraction, fill and LVS engine rests on a small geometry kernel: exact Booleans, sizing, edge and polygon predicates on integer coordinates. In an agent-first engine that kernel is the immutable core, and everything that varies between customers and runs (strategies, rule values, metrics, tiling) sits in layers around it. Deciding what belongs in the core, and how the seams around it are shaped, determines whether agents can customize the engine safely and quickly.

## What belongs in the geometry core

The core holds what must be correct for every caller: Boolean operations on polygon sets, sizing, merging, the orientation and incircle predicates, coordinate transforms, and the invariants on their outputs (simple, non-overlapping, correctly oriented rings with all vertices on the grid). A bug here is a silent sign-off escape in every rule that uses the operation, so the core is small, exhaustively tested and changed only with human approval and full regression. Anything that is a choice rather than a fact stays out: which rule to run, which metric a rule uses, how a layer is tiled. A useful test is to ask whether two reasonable customers could want different behaviour; if so, it is not core.

## Policies, parameters and hooks around it

Around the core sit three layers. Policies are strategies selected from a library or added as plug-ins: global sweep versus tiled processing, the order in which rules run, a fill-placement heuristic, a candidate-pair filter. Parameters are values with no code change: rule distances, density windows, tile size and halo, worker counts. Observation hooks expose live state, such as per-tile violation counts, density maps and progress, which an agent reads to decide what to run next. Example: a team wanting fill to prefer regions away from critical nets writes a placement policy that calls the core's NOT and sizing operations; it never edits the Boolean kernel, so a mistake in it can misplace fill but cannot corrupt a Boolean result elsewhere.

## Keeping the hot loop inside the core

Geometry engines spend their time in tight inner loops over edges and candidate pairs. If an extension point sits inside that loop, say a virtual callback per edge pair, call overhead and lost inlining can slow a check by an order of magnitude. Seams must be coarse: the core hands a plug-in a batch of candidates as plain arrays and receives a batch of results, or calls a policy once per tile. Plain data, a frozen interface and no hidden global state let the core change internally without breaking plug-ins and keep plug-ins from mutating kernel state. A second implementation of the core, such as a GPU back end, is held to the same standard: identical results on the same input, proved by differential tests.

## Going deeper

The Boost.Polygon and KLayout documentation, for examples of a compact geometry kernel with layered APIs; Parnas, "On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules" (Communications of the ACM, 1972).

C) The kernel uses integer arithmetic

D) The seam is too fine-grained: the hot inner loop crosses the plug-in boundary per pair

problems.e: Seams should be coarse (per batch or per tile) so the inner loop stays inside the core where the compiler can inline and vectorize it.

Which plug-in interface for a custom spacing measurement keeps the core fast?

A) The plug-in receives the whole flat layout as text

B) The core calls the plug-in once per vertex

C) The plug-in queries the database one shape at a time through a remote call

D) The core hands the plug-in a batch of candidate edge pairs and receives a batch of flags
problems.a: The core hands the plug-in a batch of candidate edge pairs and receives a batch of flags
problems.e: Batch interfaces amortize call overhead and keep data in plain arrays, so the core still controls memory layout and parallelism.

label: Change tiers for geometry-engine requests
prereqs: The geometry kernel as a protected core
lesson:
# Change tiers for geometry-engine requests

Requests to change a geometry engine arrive constantly: a new process value, a new rule shape, a performance problem, a bug. An agent that edits the engine should land each request at the smallest safe tier: configuration, a plug-in at an existing seam, or, rarely and under review, the core. Classifying requests correctly, and knowing what evidence each tier needs, is the practical skill. Repeated core edits for one kind of request are a sign that a seam is missing.

## Tier 1: rule decks and parameters

Most requests change values that the engine already reads: a spacing from 40 to 38 nm, density windows of 50 um, a choice between built-in metrics, a worker count, a tile size. These are Tier 1: no code changes, no recompile, and the risk is limited to the value being wrong. The evidence needed is that the intended check results change and nothing else does, which a rerun on reference layouts shows. A parallelism setting is Tier 1 with a special obligation: results must not depend on it, which golden tests verify by running at several worker counts. An agent should always look for a Tier 1 solution first, because most customer differences are differences in numbers, not in algorithms.

## Tier 2: plug-ins at a seam

When a request needs new logic that fits an existing extension point, it is Tier 2. A spacing rule that depends on whether both wires share a net and on their summed widths becomes a new spacing provider, given the pair's widths, nets and run length. A fill policy that avoids analog regions subtracts keep-outs with core Booleans. A new sweep ordering for cache behaviour plugs into an ordering interface. The core is untouched, and the evidence is golden tests plus a differential run: for a new rule, only the expected new markers appear; for a performance policy, the output is identical to the baseline with zero XOR. The harness can then promote the plug-in into the library, where other agents can select it.

## Tier 3: touching the kernel

Tier 3 changes what the core represents or computes: curvilinear primitives for photonics, wider coordinates for very large dies, a fix for a Boolean bug at a vertex shared by three polygons. These go through a human-approved diff and full regression, and a bug fix always adds the failing input as a permanent golden case. Patching around a kernel bug in a plug-in hides it from every other caller and is the wrong answer. Even changes that look small, such as widening the coordinate type, are Tier 3 because they alter overflow bounds, memory layout and every interface that carries coordinates. When the same kind of request keeps reaching Tier 3, the varying part should move behind a new seam so the next one is Tier 2.

## Going deeper

The four-layer engine model and change tiers taught in this curriculum's agent-first EDA domain; Fowler, "Refactoring" (2nd ed., 2018), on introducing seams for change.

problems.q:
A run takes too long, and the agent raises the worker count from 16 to 64. Which tier?

A) Tier 2: a new scheduling plug-in

B) Tier 3: changing the tile halo formula

C) Tier 3: rewriting the sweep for threads

D) Tier 1: a parallelism parameter
problems.a: Tier 1: a parallelism parameter
problems.e: Thread count is a run-time setting. Results must not depend on it, which the golden tests check.

problems.q:
A user wants density windows of 50 um with a 25 um step instead of 100 um with a 50 um step. Which tier?

A) Tier 3: a change to area computation

B) Tier 2: a new density policy

C) Tier 1: window and step are parameters

D) Tier 3: a change to the clipping kernel
problems.a: Tier 1: window and step are parameters
problems.e: Window and step sizes are inputs to an existing density check, so no code changes.

problems.q:
An agent switches a check from Euclidean to square (L-infinity) measurement for a quick pre-check run. Which tier, assuming both metrics are already implemented?

A) Tier 2: writing a new metric

B) Tier 3: changing the predicate kernel

C) It cannot be done without a new rule deck language

D) Tier 1: selecting an existing option
problems.a: Tier 1: selecting an existing option
problems.e: Choosing among built-in metrics is configuration. Only a metric the engine does not have would need a plug-in.

problems.q:
A team wants a custom sort order for edges in the sweep to improve cache behaviour, through an ordering interface the engine already exposes. Which tier, and what must the tests show?

A) Tier 3; any change to ordering changes results

B) Tier 1; no testing is needed for performance changes

C) Tier 2; the output may change slightly but must stay within 1 percent

D) Tier 2; the output must be identical to the baseline, with only runtime changing
problems.a: Tier 2; the output must be identical to the baseline, with only runtime changing
problems.e: An ordering policy must not change the result of an exact sweep. A differential test with zero XOR is the acceptance criterion.

problems.q:
A customer wants fill shapes to avoid a list of sensitive analog regions. The fill engine exposes a placement-policy interface. Which tier?

A) Tier 3: a change to how fill squares are sized

B) Tier 3: a change to the density computation

C) Tier 1: one more layer in the deck

D) Tier 2: a fill-placement policy plug-in
problems.a: Tier 2: a fill-placement policy plug-in
problems.e: Deciding where fill may go is policy. It uses existing Booleans to subtract keep-out regions and leaves the kernel alone.

A customer wants fill shapes to avoid a list of sensitive analog regions. The fill engine exposes a placement-policy interface. Which tier?

B) Tier 3: a change to the density computation

C) Tier 2: a fill-placement policy plug-in

D) Tier 1: one more layer in the deck
problems.a: Tier 2: a fill-placement policy plug-in
problems.e: Deciding where fill may go is policy. It uses existing Booleans to subtract keep-out regions and leaves the kernel alone.

A) A Tier 1 parameter that ignores slivers

B) Ignore it, since slivers are below the grid

C) A Tier 3 core fix with a new golden test reproducing the case

D) A Tier 2 plug-in that patches outputs after the kernel
problems.a: A Tier 3 core fix with a new golden test reproducing the case
problems.e: Patching outputs around a kernel bug hides it from other callers. The core is fixed under review, and the failing input becomes a permanent golden case.

problems.q:
A customer needs curvilinear (non-Manhattan, non-45-degree) shapes for a photonics layer, and the kernel only supports integer polygons with straight edges. Which tier?

A) No change: curves can be stored as one long edge

B) Tier 3: the geometry representation and kernel must change

C) Tier 1: a flag that enables curves

D) Tier 2: a curve plug-in at the spacing seam
problems.a: Tier 3: the geometry representation and kernel must change
problems.e: A new primitive changes what the core represents and computes. That is a kernel change needing human approval and full regression.

problems.q:
Customers keep asking for core changes to support one kind of rule after another. What does that suggest?

A) The core should be rewritten for every customer

B) The rule deck language is too expressive

C) Agents should be allowed to edit the core without review

D) A seam is missing: the varying part should be moved behind an extension point
problems.a: A seam is missing: the varying part should be moved behind an extension point
problems.e: A seam is in the right place when Tier 3 edits essentially never happen for a kind of change. Repeated core edits show where one belongs.

label: Spatial queries as agent tools
prereqs: Engines as agent tools over MCP
lesson:
# Spatial queries as agent tools

An agent fixing violations or exploring a layout cannot read a billion shapes; it asks questions. Exposing a geometry engine's spatial queries as typed tools, over an interface such as MCP, lets a model ask what lies in a window, how far two nets are apart or where violations cluster, and get small, exact answers. The tool boundary is where units, bounds, determinism, cost and the IP boundary must all be designed explicitly.

## Typed spatial queries

A good spatial tool takes typed, unit-explicit inputs and returns structured records. A region query names the layer, the window corners and the database unit; a distance query names two nets or shapes; a violation query names a rule and a region. Free-text queries push parsing onto the model and invite misunderstandings, and whole-layer dumps overflow its context. Outputs should be records an agent can compute with: for a spacing violation, the two shapes, the measured and required distances and the marker box, so the agent can work out how far an edge must move and the harness can check the fix. Internally, each tool maps to an index query: a window query on an R-tree or grid, grown by a margin when the question is about distance.

## Bounded, deterministic results

A window over a dense region can match millions of shapes. The tool should return a bounded page, the total count, and a continuation token, so the agent knows its view is partial and can refine the window or continue. Results must be deterministic: sorted by a stable key such as layer, then coordinates, then id, so that two identical queries give identical answers and harness diffs stay meaningful. Caches must be invalidated when edits touch their region, or the agent will chase violations that no longer exist. Example: a query for metal-2 shapes in a $10 \times 10$ um window returns the first 500 of 12,400 records sorted by lower-left corner, with a token for the next page.

## Cost and safety at the tool boundary

Geometry queries range from microseconds (a small window) to hours (a full-chip XOR). Tools should be region-scoped and report a cost estimate, so a planner can check only the edited area plus its interaction halo instead of rerunning everything after every change. The engine runs next to the data, inside the design site's sandbox, so the layout never leaves the site and only queries and small results cross the boundary. Editing tools need more: an edit should go through a transaction that runs the relevant checks and a differential comparison and produces a reviewable diff before commit. A fix is complete only when the edited region and its halo show the intended change and nothing new.

## Going deeper

The Model Context Protocol specification, on tool schemas and structured results; Samet, "Foundations of Multidimensional and Metric Data Structures" (2006), on window and distance queries.

problems.q:
An agent asks for violations near a net. Which query is the right primitive to expose?

A) All violation markers in the design, filtered by the agent

B) The net's name and pin count

C) Violation markers whose bounding boxes intersect the net's shapes grown by a margin

D) A screenshot of the layout around the net
problems.a: Violation markers whose bounding boxes intersect the net's shapes grown by a margin
problems.e: Growing the net's shapes and running a window query over marker boxes returns exactly the nearby violations through the spatial index.

problems.q:
A query tool returns shape coordinates in database units. What must the tool's schema also report so an agent interprets them correctly?

A) The file format of the original layout

B) The database unit size, for example 1 DBU = 1 nm

C) The number of CPU cores used

D) The time the layout was last saved
problems.a: The database unit size, for example 1 DBU = 1 nm
problems.e: Integers mean nothing without the unit. Reporting it in the schema prevents a factor-of-1000 error between nm and um.

problems.q:

A) query(text) taking a natural-language description

B) query_region(x, y) taking one point in microns

C) query_region(layer, x1, y1, x2, y2) with coordinates in stated database units

D) dump_layer(layer) returning every shape
problems.a: query_region(layer, x1, y1, x2, y2) with coordinates in stated database units
problems.e: Typed, unit-explicit inputs make the query exact and checkable. A free-text or whole-layer interface pushes parsing and filtering onto the model.

problems.q:

A) Non-deterministic order breaks reproducible runs and diffs; sort results by a stable key

B) Order should be randomized deliberately to avoid bias

C) The index is corrupted and must be rebuilt

D) It is harmless, since order never matters
problems.a: Non-deterministic order breaks reproducible runs and diffs; sort results by a stable key
problems.e: Agents and harnesses compare outputs across runs. A stable sort (for example by layer, then coordinates, then id) makes results reproducible.

problems.q:
A window query could match two million shapes. What should the tool do?

A) Refuse the query with no information

B) Return a bounded page with a total count and a continuation token

C) Silently return the first thousand

D) Return all two million shapes in one response
problems.a: Return a bounded page with a total count and a continuation token
problems.e: Bounded pages keep responses within the model's context, while the total count and token tell the agent the result is partial and how to continue.

problems.q:
An agent runs the same region query twice and gets the shapes in different orders. Why is that a problem, and what fixes it?

A) The index is corrupted and must be rebuilt

B) Order should be randomized deliberately to avoid bias

C) Non-deterministic order breaks reproducible runs and diffs; sort results by a stable key

D) It is harmless, since order never matters
problems.a: Non-deterministic order breaks reproducible runs and diffs; sort results by a stable key
problems.e: Agents and harnesses compare outputs across runs. A stable sort (for example by layer, then coordinates, then id) makes results reproducible.

problems.q:
A model calls a whole-chip XOR tool in a loop, each call taking ten minutes. What should the tool interface offer instead?

A) The XOR result as a bitmap image

B) A rule forbidding agents from calling XOR

C) A region-scoped XOR and a cost estimate, so the agent can check only the edited area

D) A faster but approximate XOR with no error bound
problems.a: A region-scoped XOR and a cost estimate, so the agent can check only the edited area
problems.e: Most edits are local. Region scoping uses the spatial index to bound work, and a cost estimate lets the planner choose when a full run is worth it.

problems.q:
An agent may call shape-editing tools as well as query tools. Which safeguard matters most?

A) Only query results are logged

B) Edits are applied immediately to the master database

C) Edit tools accept free-form commands

D) Edits go through a transaction that runs checks and produces a reviewable diff before commit
problems.a: Edits go through a transaction that runs checks and produces a reviewable diff before commit
problems.e: Edits must be reversible and verified. A transaction with a DRC and differential check, then human approval, matches the harness loop.

A) Only query results are logged

problems.e: Edits must be reversible and verified. A transaction with a DRC and differential check, then human approval, matches the harness loop.

label: Tiled parallel geometry with halos
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Tiled parallel geometry with halos

The standard way to run geometry checks on many cores, many machines or a GPU is to cut the die into tiles and process them independently. Correctness requires each worker to see a halo around its tile at least as wide as the largest interaction distance, and to report only results it owns. The halo makes the work redundant at the borders, and the tile size trades load balance against that redundancy. These are the numbers a fast-mode engine and an agent scheduling it must reason about.

## Cutting the die into tiles

A $W \times H$ die cut into $T \times T$ tiles has $\lceil W/T \rceil \cdot \lceil H/T \rceil$ tiles, the last row and column possibly partial. Example: a $2350 \times 1180$ um die with 100 um tiles has $24 \times 12 = 288$ tiles. Each tile is an independent task, so a scheduler can spread them over threads, machines or GPU thread blocks. Load balance depends on the data, not the area: a tile over a memory array may hold a hundred times the shapes of a tile over a routing channel. Engines therefore make tiles small enough that there are many more tiles than workers, or size tiles adaptively by shape count, and they schedule the heaviest tiles first.

## Halos and ownership

A spacing check near a tile border needs shapes from the neighbouring tile. So each worker reads its tile expanded by a halo of width $h$ at least equal to the largest interaction distance of the rules it runs. A shape is therefore read by every worker whose expanded tile it overlaps. Example: tiles of 40 um with a 5 um halo, and a shape spanning $[78, 83) \times [100, 110)$: in x it meets expanded tiles 1 and 2, in y tile 2 only, so two workers read it. To avoid double reporting, each violation is owned by one tile, for example the tile containing the lower-left corner of its marker. Too small a halo silently misses violations at tile borders, which is why the halo is derived from the rule deck, never guessed.

## Halo overhead and the fast-accurate loop

Each worker processes $(T + 2h)^2$ of area for $T^2$ of owned area, an overhead of $((T + 2h)^2 - T^2)/T^2$. Example: 200 um tiles with a 5 um halo process 10.25 percent extra; 50 um tiles with the same halo process 44 percent extra. Smaller tiles balance load better and fit GPU memory, but the halo is fixed by the rules, so overhead grows as tiles shrink. This trade-off is a parameter an agent can tune in a fast mode: large tiles and a subset of rules for quick feedback during an ECO loop, then the full deck for sign-off. A GPU or tiled back end must still produce exactly the results of the serial engine, which a differential test on reference layouts verifies.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on physical verification; the KLayout documentation on tiling mode in DRC scripts.

problems.q: A parallel DRC engine cuts a 6031 by 2324 um die into 200 by 200 um tiles (the last row and column may be partial) and hands one tile to each worker. How many tiles are there?
problems.e: ceil(6031 / 200) = 31 columns and ceil(2324 / 200) = 12 rows give 372 tiles.

problems.q: A parallel DRC engine cuts a 3674 by 3858 um die into 100 by 100 um tiles (the last row and column may be partial) and hands one tile to each worker. How many tiles are there?

problems.e: ceil(5364 / 250) = 22 columns and ceil(1098 / 250) = 5 rows give 110 tiles.

problems.e: Tile i covers [20i - 4, 20(i + 1) + 4) once expanded. The shape meets 3 expanded columns and 3 expanded rows: 9 workers.

problems.q: Tiles are half-open 40 by 40 um squares on a 10 by 10 grid starting at the origin. Each worker reads its tile expanded by a halo of 2 um, the largest interaction distance. How many workers must read the shape $[212, 243) \times [149, 192)$?
problems.e: Tile i covers [40i - 2, 40(i + 1) + 2) once expanded. The shape meets 2 expanded columns and 2 expanded rows: 4 workers.

problems.e: Tile i covers [50i - 11, 50(i + 1) + 11) once expanded. The shape meets 3 expanded columns and 3 expanded rows: 9 workers.

problems.e: ((80 + 2(5))^2 - 80^2) / 80^2 = 26.6 percent of redundant work. Smaller tiles balance load better but pay more halo; the halo is fixed by the rule deck, not by the tile size.

problems.e: ((360 + 2(22))^2 - 360^2) / 360^2 = 25.9 percent of redundant work. Smaller tiles balance load better but pay more halo; the halo is fixed by the rule deck, not by the tile size.

problems.q: Tiles are 260 by 260 um and each worker processes its tile plus a 1 um halo on every side. By what percent does the processed area exceed the tile area? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: ((260 + 2(1))^2 - 260^2) / 260^2 = 1.5 percent of redundant work. Smaller tiles balance load better but pay more halo; the halo is fixed by the rule deck, not by the tile size.

label: Differential testing of geometry engines
prereqs: Area of a union of rectangles by sweep
lesson:
# Differential testing of geometry engines

When an agent or an engineer changes a geometry engine, the proof that nothing broke is differential: run the old and new versions on reference layouts and compare the outputs geometrically. For polygon outputs the comparison is an XOR, and the expected result is usually empty. The size and shape of a nonzero XOR say exactly what changed, which makes it the acceptance test for every tier of change.

## XOR of two outputs

For a golden output $G$ and a new output $N$ on the same layer, the differential region is $G \oplus N$, with area $|G| + |N| - 2|G \cap N|$. Example: a golden shape $[2, 12] \times [3, 9]$ and a new shape $[2, 13] \times [3, 9]$ have areas 60 and 66 and overlap 60, so the XOR area is 6, a one-unit strip along the right edge. A performance change, a refactoring or a new back end must give an XOR of exactly zero on every reference layout. A rule change must give an XOR confined to where the rule was meant to act. Because the comparison is geometric, it ignores irrelevant differences such as vertex order or the starting point of a ring, which a text diff of output files would flag.

## Comparing whole layers

Real outputs are sets of shapes, and the comparison must be between unions, not shape lists. Two engines can produce different decompositions of the same region, for example one rectangle against two abutting ones, and still be equivalent; the union XOR is zero. Conversely, a change to one shape can be partly hidden by another shape that overlaps it, so the XOR can be smaller than a per-shape diff suggests. Example: golden shapes whose union covers 180 units and a new set in which one rectangle grew by 2 units along a 7-unit edge, half of that growth landing inside another shape, give an XOR of 7, not 14. The engine computes the XOR with the same sweep it uses for any Boolean, and reports markers for the differing regions.

## Reading the signature of a change

The shape of a nonzero XOR identifies the bug. A uniform shift of every shape by $\delta$ in x produces, for each rectangle of height $h$ and width greater than $\delta$, two slivers of $\delta \times h$, an XOR of $2\delta h$ per shape: a structured, layout-wide pattern that points at a coordinate transform or rounding change. Example: shifting shapes of heights 4, 7 and 10 by 2 units gives $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 21 = 84$. A sizing bug shows as thin rings around every shape, a Boolean bug as isolated slivers at special vertices. A good harness reports XOR area per layer and per region, the number of markers, and thresholds that block promotion, so an agent's change is accepted only when the differential matches its stated intent.

## Going deeper

McKeeman, "Differential testing for software" (Digital Technical Journal, 1998); the KLayout documentation on the XOR tool for layout comparison.

problems.q: A regression compares a golden output shape $[3, 14] \times [7, 13]$ with a new engine's output $[10, 15] \times [2, 9]$. What is the area of their XOR, the region the differential check reports?
